item.title: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii (162 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://virtuallyfun.com/2026/10/29/my-favourite-powermac-is-a-nintendo-wii/, See on Hacker News

(This is a guest post by Rairii)

So today I reached a nice milestone in one of my projects: my work porting classic Mac OS to PowerPC systems with what I affectionately call ArtX chipsets (Nintendo GameCube, Wii, eventually Wii U; the GameCube’s Flipper integrated chipset was very much designed by ArtX as it was effectively finished when ATI acquired the company, and the Wii’s Vegas (and its later revision Bollywood) and Wii U’s Latte are effectively straight successors) reached the desktop for the first time, most likely the first time since the CHRP clone era that someone outside of Apple brought up classic Mac OS on a new system to the desktop. Despite still being nowhere near ready for a public release, I want to talk about the challenges I faced with this project so far.

But first, why port classic Mac OS to this hardware in the first place? I’d already ported NT of course, and during that work I acquired some PowerPC Mac laptops which I also ended up porting NT to, work on one port improved the others and so on. This got me acquainted with the classic Mac OS, and I fell in love with the jank as it were (hacks upon hacks upon hacks going back to the 1980s is something I’d definitely describe as “jank”). Not to mention the m68k part of the TBXI is called “SuperMario”, and was for the entire PowerPC era. I wonder if a developer was a fan in the early 1990s?

Also, for the record: I started this project on 2025-06-22 (when I forked upstream openbios), no kind of coding agent or LLM was used, all coding, reversing and debugging work done by myself. I do these projects for fun and to learn, if I used “AI” it wouldn’t be fun and I wouldn’t learn anything.

Let’s start with the initial boot. “New World” classic Mac OS starts out with a bootloader called the “Trampoline”, which runs on an Open Firmware environment. So I needed to port OpenBIOS. Luckily, around this time Goldfish64 had started his own port of Mac OS X to the Wii, and he’d made an OpenBIOS port that I could use some drivers from, although for various reasons I didn’t just want to use his port directly (which was only targeting Wii/Wii U, I wanted to target GameCube too). I also decided to reuse some existing code to make some driver development easier (specifically the display driver), and thus changed my existing NT ARC firmware loader to load a big endian ELF instead.

I needed some small number of disk drivers for initial bringup, so decided to port my two drivers for devices on the EXI bus (this is just Nintendo and Macronix’s name for SPI), the “SD Gecko” (which is just a straight through adapter for a GameCube memory card slot allowing for SD over SPI), and the “EXI-IDE” (my driver is actually not correct to real hardware, but to my inaccurate emulation in my Dolphin tree allowing for testing under emulator with the low level debugging support that implies).

I wasn’t sure what kind of on-disk format I wanted to use (these drivers on my earlier NT port ran entirely using disk images on a FAT filesystem, due to the requirement for compatibiltiy with existing homebrew loaders that load executables from FAT filesystems, but this would naturally be limited to 4GB images for FAT32, and later versions of classic Mac OS needed more), so for initial testing I just took the “Mac OS ROM” TBXI file and placed it directly on a FAT filesystem as \ppc\bootinfo.txt for OpenBIOS to load it on boot.

So with that I could get the Trampoline running. I decided that I should try and apply as many patches to the image as possible as close to run-time as possible, so mostly untouched existing CD images could be used eventually.

The first issue I had was that the Trampoline makes some assumptions of the physical address space layout that are not true for this system. The physical address of a buffer gets calculated as an invalid address, so I patched that to an address guaranteed to be valid, and also the corresponding code setting up the memory chunk list/page table entries for the kernel.

Additionally, the Trampoline expects that physical addresses from 0x8000_0000 onwards corresponds to memory mapped I/O (on existing systems this code ran on, this would correspond to PCI-bus address space). This is not the case here, and in fact on Wii U, this address would correspond to part of RAM. There was also another assumption that broke on these systems, with holes between areas of RAM in the physical address space, some of which were partially filled by memory-mapped I/O.

The way I fixed this was to patch the initialisation of this MMIO mapping in the kernel memory chunk list, to a map of physical address 0x0100_0000 (partway through one area of RAM) to virtual address 0xE000_0000, with length 0x1000_0000. This specifically maps the whole of the MMIO, plus the end of one RAM area and (for post-GameCube systems) the start of another. (I may change this in future, as on the Wii U, physical address range 0xD000_0000-0xEFFF_FFFF is mapped to a part of the Radeon R7xx GPU called “HDP”, which can be used to map a view of physical memory with specific swizzling and/or endianness swapping, such that a texture in some GPU-specific format can appear to be a linear framebuffer. It depends on whether I need to use this block ) The function used for initialising a mapping in the Trampoline changed at some point and I ended up detecting the older version and hooking the function so I could work around it (earlier versions used a 16-bit page count, later versions used 32-bit). Additionally, older versions of the Trampoline sets up unconditional 1:1 mappings for physical memory above 0x8000_0000, which needs to be removed as they conflict with the mappings set up earlier.

There follows various assorted patches that assume specific hardware. These include: patching out setting some bitflags which correspond to the presence of a microcontroller found on all PowerPC Macintosh hardware, attempting to recalculate the bus frequency using a specific hardware timer, and various register writes and fixups related to a specific interrupt controller device (it’s little endian because it’s on the PCI bus, and naturally, not present here).

Finally, the final call to jump into the loaded kernel initialisation code is hooked so additional patches can be made later after everything is loaded into memory.

Additionally, the device tree must be hacked up a bit to be in a shape the Trampoline will accept. The interrupt controller is faked to be one of the recognised ones (the little endian one from above, because at a register level it’s closest to the Flipper interrupt controller present on all the ArtX chipsets, albeit on Wii U it was changed somewhat to add support for the additional PowerPC cores). The address of the frame buffer in the device tree is changed to the uncached virtual address (in the 0xExxx_xxxx mapping), and finally a fake Mac99-compatible power management device is added to the device tree, so the Trampoline prepares a power management driver for it, that can be replaced later.

As mentioned above, the kernel initialisation is hooked so extra patches can be made. On the kernel side, there is only one patch to be made: the kernel contains several interrupt controller drivers, the one chosen is patched to match the Flipper interrupt controller, with one of the unused ones sacrificed to gain more space for this. The main difference here is that the expected interrupt controller (whose driver is patched) has a legacy mode where it raises a PowerPC interrupt whenever the interrupts change (not just when interrupts are raised) so this needs to be worked around by masking the raised interrupts in the kernel and then unmasking them later on in drivers’ interrupt handlers.

Additional patches are made in the “SuperMario” m68k code, and in PowerPC native executables. The m68k code has various codepaths that read and write directly to native interrupt controller registers, these need to be patched. The function pointers for enabling and disabling audio interrupts need to be stubbed out (there’s already an entry in that table that points to a stub, which is helpful). A function called early in the boot process to initialise the ADB and power management microcontroller does not check if the hardware actually exists, and if it doesn’t it clobbers parts of low memory. A function for initialising hardware interrupts has a bug due to a copy-paste blunder, the intent was to skip past the code for initialising the interrupt for serial port 2 if the hardware isn’t present, but the developers forgot to change the jump label when copy-pasting the code from serial port 1, which causes an infinite loop if serial port 2 doesn’t exist. As for native code, there’s more code that reads and writes to interrupt controller registers which needs to be correctly patched. The USBShimKeyboard driver initialisation code fails to handle the state where no USB controller exists and in that case will call a NULL pointer inside the m68k emulator. The power management driver mentioned above is also replaced entirely here (currently I use the stub driver from BlueBox but plan to write my own later to add proper support for shutting down and restarting).

All of this is enough to get the TBXI to boot to blinking floppy – after that I wrote a display driver (thanks to Elliott Nunn for his virtio driver, it was very helpful) so I could see it correctly, followed by a driver for the gamecube controller ports (porting from my NT driver for the same) so I could move the mouse cursor around without USB.

At this point I started to implement a block IO driver (for EXI devices), but ended up getting stuck thinking about how to deal with how the disk format should be laid out and how the driver should work. Then Mac OS for CHRP got dumped, and I got sidetracked with patching up the later TBXI images to boot it, thinking running 7.x would be useful on a GameCube which doesn’t even have enough RAM to support 8.0 at minimum requirements, and after that I got sidetracked with other projects. Almost a year later I came back to it, implemented my preferred disk format in OpenBIOS and decided to hack up a driver faking SCSI (some other drivers did this, most notably classic Mac OS drivers for various SATA controllers). There were a few issues I found when writing the fake-SCSI driver too: I had to add another patch to the m68k code to force loading the disk driver (and I mean this, a driver loaded from the disk itself, basically implementing the actual disk devices on top of some partitioned block device) as a newer type rather than the older type (the older type was effectively obsolete when the first PowerPC systems released anyway, and I don’t even support the old-style calls from my fake SCSI driver, which is probably why it crashed trying to load it as an older type driver), and also found an interesting quirk where the optical disc driver (loaded from the block device itself) emulates 512-byte sectors on 2048- or 2352-byte sector block devices by making a read call setting up 3 scatter-gather buffers, except it never checked if the underlying SCSI driver actually supports scatter-gather, so I had to implement support for that on reads.

I still saw a blinking floppy though, some debugging showed me what was being rejected, a PowerPC function StartLib!GetStartupDevice was being called to get the boot device, and it made some assumptions of both the device tree and that there was some kind of built in SCSI device that needed separate handling. The first one was simple enough (fix the device tree in my driver’s initialisation code), the second one was more interesting in that I had to grovel into internal structures to fix an index in 3 different places (including the device tree) to ensure it was non-zero and so the correct code path would be executed.

With this done I saw a happy Mac icon for the first time, but then got rejected by the HFS boot sector (something errored and it returned). This turned out to be a bug in my own driver: I was debugging in dolphin with a hacked up EXI-IDE device; reading and writing data in PIO mode for IDE devices deals in 16-bit words, and I didn’t expect my code to get passed a completely unaligned odd buffer address (low 4 bits equal to 1), so I had to modify my low level driver to not even attempt EXI DMA for such an address. The bug manifested as a byte effectively failing to be written out, with remaining data getting offset by one byte; at least this happened when reading the header of a resource fork, and what failed was the validity checks for this data, making it much easier to debug (I ended up dumping RAM and comparing with the expected data from the disk image I was using).

After this, Mac OS 9.2.2 started to boot in my hacked up Dolphin tree, very slowly. It took an hour before it finally crashed, and then I tried 7.6, which also crashed, but earlier. I realised that it was probably crashing trying to load MacsBug, removed it, and after about 20 minutes I was staring at the desktop.

The following morning I tested on real hardware (using SD over SPI). This basically booted 7.6 within 40 seconds, and this was supposed to be the slowest access mode for an SD card! My previous experience was writing an NT driver for SD over SPI though, and perhaps that is more of an outlier. See this video installing NT on a GameCube using such a block device, and note that the NT text setup file copy is sped up 64 times – it’s VERY slow. The difference here is that I get to hog the whole CPU when performing a transfer – in fact there’s no other option, if I return a value specifying the transfer is asynchronous, the caller proceeds to busy-wait for interrupts in a loop waiting for the transfer to complete (although the busy-wait does check for all controllers present on the system).

Later on I added some hacked up crash handler so I could try to debug what was going on with MacsBug… it turned out to be an emulation error, no such crash occured when loading MacsBug on real hardware. I then found out the reason Mac OS 9.2.2 was crashing on boot was because of Open Transport, removing it from the Extensions folder caused it to boot perfectly fine. My guess is that Open Transport can’t handle no serial or network device being present at all.

As I mentioned, my port is still nowhere near release. Next up will be bringing up the Wii’s SD controller, then the USB controller (I’ve already done some reversing work related to that, I know there’s a vibecoded EHCI driver now, that’ll probably only aid in reversing work really), then getting the port brought up on the Wii U. At some point I want to play around with patches for blowing through at least some of the RAM barriers too.

item.title: Proton's CEO Cancels AI 'Re-Interviews' (232 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.404media.co/protons-ceo-cancels-ai-re-interviews/, See on Hacker News

On Friday, Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, cancelled a series of nearly company-wide ‘re-interviews’ that would have forced employees to explain how they are using AI, with the clear intention that they may be fired if not using it enough in the eyes of Proton leadership, according to six current Proton employees and audio of an around two hour all-hands meeting obtained by 404 Media.

The move came after 404 Media published an investigation on Thursday, which showed how Yen was aggressively pushing AI across Proton, in some cases despite security concerns from employees. In one exchange, an employee in the company’s security Slack channel urged Proton to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” Yen added, “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

The re-interview cancellations likely don’t address the concerns of many Proton users, who are more focused on Proton’s deprioritization of security; many Proton users have blasted the company’s leadership on social media over the last 24 hours and explicitly called for Yen to resign.

The investigation was based on conversations with eight current and one former Proton employees, Slack chats, meeting audio, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO Bart Butler. It painted a picture of Proton that is very different to the public’s perception of a company carefully protecting privacy. Instead, Proton is barreling ahead with AI in large part to achieve more annual revenue. The investigation also found a culture of fear across Proton, where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security-focused products with AI, but feel unable to voice them because Yen mocks or insults employees in front of everyone else.

“I don’t think he will change anything, and I think the only reason we had this meeting is because he has a rebellion on his hands,” one employee told 404 Media after the all-hands meeting on Friday.

Near the start of the meeting, Yen said, “I want to acknowledge myself, personally, that there was a communication failure on my part and there are many things that probably could and should have been communicated differently, and this is something that I’ll have to reflect on and improve over time. So I will do that.”

“So what does that mean going forward? Going forward, I'm still going to push,” he added.

Yen said leadership gathered in the last couple of days to talk about the re-interviews, and spoke to the Proton board too. “They’re closely monitoring the situation,” Yen said. (Proton is owned by the Proton Foundation, whose board of trustees includes Yen, Sir Tim Berners Lee, Prof. Carissa Veliz, Dingchao Lu, and Antonio Gambardella.) 

After those discussions with leadership and the board, “We’ve decided to actually cancel the re-interviews,” Yen said. “Why? Well, I think actually in a, let’s say, unintentional way, they have actually already served their purpose.” As in, employees are now talking and learning about AI.

💡

Do you know anything else about Proton? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.

Yen also mentioned “org changes,” and said that part of this is “redistributing talent across teams.” He said that the reorganization will happen next month, “but there will be no loss of jobs from AI.” 

Later in the call, Butler said Yen “needs to, and he has committed to, doing better” regarding how he communicates with his employees. “Using AI effectively and pragmatically does not mean that we’ve given up on security, or good architecture, or sound software engineering principles,” he added.

“We fucked up, we know we fucked up,” Butler later said in response to an employee’s comments in the meeting.

“Your old job is gone,” Butler’s AI manifesto, posted to Slack, told engineers, 404 Media reported on Thursday. He wrote that not embracing AI posed an “existential threat to the success of the mission itself.”

Reactions to the re-interview cancellations were split across the Proton employees 404 Media spoke to. One said, “Some are happy as it’s progress. Others believe that this won’t change anything because there isn’t any consequence for Andy [Yen].” The employee added they “would have preferred real accountability from the leadership team.” They said they felt not much could have happened due to Yen having the majority of Proton’s shares.

Another employee said, after Proton canceled the re-interviews, “They said in the next breath they want to continue pushing AI and that the things that were to be measured in the re-interviews would become a component of the performance reviews.”

“They have said clearly the direction had not changed. As a Proton user that doesn’t reassure me,” the employee said. “As an employee, the re-interviews weren’t cancelled until this became public despite concerns raised by many of us. I think it goes beyond communication issues and growing pains.”

“Right now, everything seems consistent with it being damage control,” they said. 

Another employee said they were “mostly happy with how this was addressed including by Andy [Yen].”

Proton did not respond to a request for comment.

After 404 Media published the investigation on Thursday, Yen took to Reddit. Users downvoted his response more than 1,200 times. Many Proton users on social media said they were cancelling their paid Proton plans.

About the author

Joseph is an award-winning investigative journalist focused on generating impact. His work has triggered hundreds of millions of dollars worth of fines, shut down tech companies, and much more.

item.title: A Working Nintendo in ~1GB of Qwen Weights (142 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/dbreunig/nesformer, See on Hacker News

An NES CPU compiled into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 model.

The NES's 6502 CPU (the core of its 2A03 chip), its 2 KB of work RAM, and a cartridge's program ROM run inside a standard Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint. Nobody trained these weights; a compiler computed every one. When you play a game, the model predicts the CPU's execution log one token at a time. A small host program plays the rest of the console around it: it draws the picture, reads the controller, and fires the vblank interrupt.

nesformer builds on Qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, which compiled a CHIP-8 and then a RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B. It reuses Qwenputer's compiler and its central trick: the model's Gated DeltaNet state is the machine's memory.

Super Mario Bros. (World 1-1) Full Game by Doug Fraker (title screen and first level)

Every CPU token in these runs came from the model. For the bundled test games, every frame also matches a conventional 6502 emulator's output exactly (see How it was checked).

Quick start

1. Folder layout

Unzip nesformer.zip and nesformer-weights.zip into the same folder. The weights go next to the nesformer/ package, not inside it:

nesformer/              <- run commands from here
├── nesformer/          <- the Python package
├── chipformer/         <- Qwenputer's compiler
├── roms/               <- test ROMs (put your own here too)
├── examples/           <- sample GIFs and frame sheets
├── tests/
├── LICENSE
├── LICENSE.chipformer
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
└── weights/            <- from nesformer-weights.zip
    ├── config.json
    ├── generation_config.json
    ├── model.safetensors
    ├── nesformer.json
    └── SHA256SUMS

The CLI looks for weights/ beside the nesformer/ package. To keep the weights elsewhere, pass --weights /path/to/weights to run, check or trace, or give the path to info.

To confirm the weights unzipped correctly, run shasum -a 256 -c weights/SHA256SUMS from the top folder.

2. Install

You need Python 3.11 or newer.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install numpy scipy numba pillow

3. Play a game

python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 600 --show \
  --buttons "start@90-95+200-205,a@230-233+250-253+270-273+290-293+310-313+330-333+350-353+370-373+390-393+410-413+430-433+450-453+470-473+490-493+510-513+530-533+550-553+570-573+590-593"

--show draws each frame in your terminal as the model generates it. When the run ends, the CLI saves an animated GIF named after the ROM (here thwaite.gif) in the current folder.

Expect it to be slow. The first run spends about 20 seconds compiling the engine with numba. After that, a frame takes 1–6 seconds, so 600 frames (10 seconds of NES time) take around 25 minutes.

Playing your own ROMs

Point run at any .nes file that uses the NROM board (iNES mapper 0), such as Super Mario Bros., Donkey Kong or Excitebike. You supply the ROM; nesformer only ships the three freely licensed test ROMs in roms/.

python -m nesformer run roms/smb.nes --frames 600 --show \
  --buttons "start@60-65,right@200-600,a@250-265+300-315+360-375+420-435+480-495+540-555"

That script starts the game, then walks Mario right and jumps about once a second. The CLI loads the ROM into the model's state at startup, so the same weights run any NROM game without a rebuild. Games on other boards stop with a message: see Limitations.

Controller scripts

--buttons takes a comma-separated list of entries. Each entry names one or more buttons joined by +, then @, then one or more frame ranges joined by +:

start@60-65                 press Start during frames 60 to 65
right@200-600               hold Right from frame 200 to frame 600
a@250-265+300-315           press A twice
right+b@200-600             hold Right and B together (run, in Super Mario Bros.)

The buttons are a, b, select, start, up, down, left and right. Frames count from power-on at 60 per second, so frame 600 is 10 seconds in. Games ignore input on screens where you can't move, so holding a button a little early does no harm. In Super Mario Bros., a longer A press makes a higher jump.

Commands

Command What it does
python -m nesformer run ROM Play a ROM on the weights and save a GIF
python -m nesformer check ROM Run the weights and the reference CPU side by side; stop at the first difference
python -m nesformer trace ROM Print the model's token stream (default 40 tokens)
python -m nesformer build Compile the circuit and write weights/ (about 10 seconds)
python -m nesformer info Describe the checkpoint

Options for run:

Option Default Meaning
--frames N 120 Stop after N frames
--buttons SCRIPT none Controller input (see above)
--show off Draw frames in the terminal (needs 24-bit color, e.g. iTerm2 or Windows Terminal)
--gif PATH ROM name Where to save the animated GIF
--png DIR off Save each kept frame as a PNG in DIR. With --png alone, no GIF is saved. Add --gif to get both.
--every N 1 Keep every N-th frame
--scale N 2 Enlarge saved frames N times
--engine fast fast (numba), numpy, or hf (stock transformers; needs torch, ~10 tokens/s)
--no-skip off Run every iteration of idle wait loops (slower; identical frames)
--max-tokens N none Stop after N tokens
--trace FILE none Save the token ids

run, check and trace all accept --weights, --engine, --buttons and --no-skip. check --tokens N sets how far to compare (default 50,000). trace --tokens N sets how many tokens to print (default 40). build --out DIR writes the checkpoint somewhere other than weights/.

How it works

What's in the weights, and what isn't

In the model (weights + DeltaNet state) In the host (nesformer/host.py)
The 6502 core: all 151 official opcodes, every addressing mode, flags, stack, BRK and NMI entry The PPU: a scanline renderer and the palette
2 KB of work RAM Controllers; APU registers (written, otherwise ignored)
32 KB of PRG-ROM, stored twice: one copy for instruction fetch, one for data reads NMI timing at vblank, injected as an NMI token
OAM DMA reads (the 256 bytes appear as DM tokens) Answers to I/O reads, injected as IN tokens

This split follows Qwenputer's CHIP-8 build, whose host injects timer ticks and draws the display from the trace. The host never sees the CPU's registers or RAM except through the trace.

The memory trick works like this. Each DeltaNet head keeps a 128 × 128 state matrix that the delta rule updates at every token. With the gate held open and a one-hot key, an update overwrites exactly one row of that matrix, and a one-hot query reads it back. So every row is a memory cell, and the cartridge, RAM and registers all live in rows.

The checkpoint

weights/ is an ordinary Hugging Face folder. It loads with Qwen3_5ForCausalLM.from_pretrained and needs no custom code.
Architecture Qwen3_5ForCausalLM, with Qwen3.5-4B's DeltaNet head shapes (16 key heads, 32 value heads, dim 128) and MLP width (9,216)
Layers 7 Gated DeltaNet layers (the circuit), plus 1 all-zero attention layer that Hugging Face's cache needs
Hidden size 768
Vocabulary 263,808 tokens
Parameters 466.6M in bf16 (933 MB), of which 9.3M are nonzero, so the weights zip to 3.3 MB

nesformer.json records which layer and head holds each part of the machine. A run writes the cartridge, registers and RAM into those DeltaNet states, then decodes greedily.

Layer plan

Layer Attention (state) MLP
1 PC anchor; instruction counters; A, X, Y, SP; flags N V Z C I D; pointer latches; NMI flag counter thermometers; SP ± 1; LO + Y
2 — PC = anchor + bytes executed since; PC + 1, PC + 2
3 PRG fetch: opcode and two operand bytes at the PC opcode decode; operand bits; indexed sums; branch test and target
4 — effective address, by addressing mode and record stage; the byte a push stores
5 RAM and PRG data reads at the effective address operand; ADC/SBC adder, compares, BIT; address decode
6 — result byte, carry, overflow, flags, jump targets
7 — the next token

The trace

Each instruction becomes a record, and the record's last token commits it. As in Qwenputer's RISC-V core, the PC is implied rather than written: each final token carries its instruction's length, three DeltaNet counters tally the instructions of each length since the last jump, and the PC is the jump target plus that offset. Excerpts from Full Game:

SEI            P(000100 px0 L1)
LDX #$40       X($40 c0 v0 px0 L2)
STX $4017      IOW($4017=$40 L3)
TXS            S($FF L1)
BIT $2002      IOR($2002) IN($00) P(000110 px0 L3)       <- the host injects IN
BPL $8017      J($8017)
JSR $8279      PSH($FE) PSH($FD) J($8279)                 <- the return address is pushed in-circuit
RTS            PUL($FC) LO($7B) PUL($FD) J($827C)
STA ($72),Y    LO($08) HI($03) ST($00 a7=0 L2)            <- pointer bytes latched, then the store
STA $4014      IOW($4014=$02 L0) DM(0:$FF) … DM(255:$00) NT(L3)   <- OAM DMA

Most instructions take a single token; real game code averages 1.1–1.3 tokens per instruction. nesformer/spec.py documents every token family.

How it was checked

  • The reference CPU (nesformer/cpu.py) matches nestest's golden log for 3,348 instructions, and the py65 emulator on 5.7 million instructions of game code.

  • The exact circuit, run in Qwenputer's evaluator with its bf16 exactness checks, predicts every reference token: all of nestest plus 283,610 positions of two games' boot sequences.

  • The checkpoint in stock transformers (bf16, CPU) predicts 2,651 positions of nestest and Full Game with no mismatches.

  • The weights, free-running, generate traces identical to the reference CPU's:

    Run Tokens Frames NES time Result
    nestest (official opcodes) 4,586 — — identical, ending in the expected HALT
    Thwaite, check 700,000 271 4.5 s identical trace and frames
    Thwaite, run 1,916,527 600 10.0 s all 300 saved frames match
    Full Game, run 2,645,885 420 7.0 s all 210 saved frames match

  • The idle-loop skip changes nothing visible: frames and I/O writes, cycle timestamps included, match a run without it.

Speed

The default engine computes Qwen3.5's forward pass from model.safetensors, compiled with numba and skipping the all-zero blocks. It ran at about 1,650 tokens/s on one CPU core of the machine it was built on. The plain numpy engine does about 210, and stock transformers about 10. A real NES would need about 700,000 tokens per second.

Games spend most of each frame in a loop that waits for vblank. When the host sees a loop body repeat exactly, with no RAM or I/O writes, it advances the clock to just before the next PPU event, and the remaining iterations still run. That cuts the token count by 2.6× to 4.2×. Overall, nesformer runs 150–290× slower than the real console.

Limitations

  • NROM cartridges only (iNES mapper 0). The CPU can address only 32 KB of program ROM at a time. Bigger games carry a bank-switching chip (a mapper, such as MMC1 or MMC3) that swaps which part of the ROM the CPU sees. nesformer's ROM reads happen inside the model, from a fixed 32 KB table, so it can't follow a bank switch yet. Supporting a mapper means storing the whole ROM in the state, keeping the bank registers there too, and adding one stage that turns each CPU address into a ROM address.
  • Official opcodes only. An unofficial opcode emits HALT.
  • Code must run from the cartridge ROM. A jump into RAM emits HALT.
  • No IRQs (APU frame IRQ, DMC). BRK and NMI work.
  • Read-modify-write instructions on I/O registers don't produce an I/O write, and $4020–$7FFF reads as 0 (no PRG-RAM).
  • The PPU and APU aren't in the weights. The PPU renders one scanline at a time, so mid-scanline effects aren't reproduced. Sprite-0 hit and sprite overflow are approximate, and there's no sound.

Tests

pip install pytest py65
python -m pytest -q tests

The tests take a few minutes. They check the reference CPU against nestest's log, the circuit against the reference, the weights free-running against the reference, and the idle-loop skip.

Running the checkpoint in stock transformers

pip install "torch>=2.6" "transformers>=5.22"
python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 3 --engine hf

nesformer/hfcheck.py shows the whole procedure: load the checkpoint, decode one padding token, write the machine's state into the cache's DeltaNet states, then feed tokens one at a time.

Files

Path Contents
nesformer/spec.py token families and records
nesformer/cpu.py the reference 6502 that writes the trace
nesformer/host.py everything around the CPU: PPU, controllers, NMI timing, cycle counting, idle skip
nesformer/core.py the circuit and the state snapshot
nesformer/weights.py the emitter that turns the circuit into a Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint
nesformer/engine.py, fastengine.py run the weights (numpy / numba)
nesformer/hfcheck.py run the weights in stock transformers
nesformer/run.py, check.py, cli.py, __main__.py drivers, the teacher-forced check, the CLI
chipformer/ Qwenputer's q35 compiler (q35/ emitter and primitives, dsl/ graph)
weights/ the compiled checkpoint and its SHA-256 checksum
roms/ test ROMs; roms/SOURCES.md lists their authors and licenses
examples/ GIFs and frame sheets from the runs; demo.gif is the Super Mario Bros. run shown at the top
tests/test_nesformer.py the test suite

Credits

  • Qwenputer and its chipformer compiler: MIT, © 2026 Divyansh Agrawal (LICENSE.chipformer). That license also covers the code adapted from Qwenputer in nesformer/core.py and nesformer/weights.py. Its last paragraph refers to Qwenputer's CHIP-8 ROMs, which this repository does not include.
  • Test ROMs: nestest by Kevin Horton; Full Game by Doug Fraker (MIT); Thwaite by Damian Yerrick (GPL-3.0, source at pinobatch/thwaite-nes).

License

nesformer is released under the MIT License (see LICENSE). The ROMs in roms/ keep their own licenses, listed in roms/SOURCES.md.

item.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears (219 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvwy72e0n72yo, See on Hacker News

Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).

Shares in Intel plummeted by as much as 30% on Friday, following Google owner Alphabet's stock price plunging by more than $500bn (£374bn) in the previous day's trading.

Other tech stocks including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, sank more than 3.5%.

While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.

Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800.6bn between them in 2026.

Alphabet's stock market value plunged on Thursday after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.

At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.

Alphabet stock continued to fall in early trading, down 2.2% after Thursday's slide of more than 12%.

The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere, with Intel on track to lose more than $130bn in value as its shares continued to fall in Friday trading.

The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.

On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.

"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.

In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.

Amazon shares fell as far as 6% in overnight trading after the company's reported earnings fell short of investors' expectations.

Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.

The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.

Shares recovered slightly from the overnight fall but were still down about 1.6% in Friday trading.

Reddit stock was down by 26%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.

Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by nearly 20%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.

Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.

Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.

He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".

"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."

Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.

The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.

Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.

"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.

"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."

However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.

While the Nasdaq is down 3.5% in Friday trading, it is up 7.6% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 7% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.6%.

Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.

"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

item.title: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them (415 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://newsletter.signoz.io/p/ai-isnt-replacing-sres-its-deskilling, See on Hacker News

💌 Hey there, it’s Elizabeth from SigNoz!

This newsletter is an honest attempt to talk about all things - observability, OpenTelemetry, open-source and the engineering in between!
&
This piece took 6 days, 5 hours to be cooked, hope we served. 🌚

There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days.

The first says SRE is the future of all software engineering, that as AI writes more and more code, the humans who remain will be the ones keeping systems alive. The second says AI will devour every tech job alive, SREs included. Neither is particularly useful if you’re an SRE trying to figure out what your Tuesday will look like in 2027.

Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?

Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient.

Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉).

In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge published a paper called Ironies of Automation. It became one of the most cited papers in human factors research, and its core argument is almost uncomfortably relevant today.

Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for.

Ring any bells yet? 🙂

Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems.

The exact problems that require deep expertise, the exact expertise that atrophies when you stop practising.

Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing.

Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering.

Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today.

Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks.

PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model.

  • Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated.

  • Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation.

  • Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context.

But here’s the catch.

If human SREs (okay, now we have to use adjectives like human 🥹) only engage with Tier 3 incidents, i.e. the novel, never-before-seen outages, where do they build the intuition to handle them? Intuition is usually developed from years of hands-on incident response, pattern recognition built through repetition, and the kind of gut-level understanding of a system that only develops from painfully waking up at the odd hour to solve the bug that brought the system down.

This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture.

In medicine, a recent study found that endoscopists who used AI assistance for polyp detection saw their unassisted detection rates drop from 28% to 22% after a period of AI use. They got worse at the thing they were supposed to be experts in, not because they forgot the theory, but because they stopped exercising the skill.

In aviation, research has shown that long-haul pilots who rely heavily on autopilot systems experience measurable degradation in situational awareness and manual flying ability. The problem got serious enough that the FAA now mandates more manual flying time to counteract the effect.

Somewhere over the past year, AI stopped being a tool I occasionally reached for and became the first thing I reach for, always. My instinct now is to offload as much as possible and apply my own thinking only where it’s absolutely unavoidable. The problem is that these moments are becoming the only exercises my brain gets, and I can feel the rust.

We can draw a pattern here. The more you let the system handle, the worse you get at handling things yourself and here’s the truly dangerous part, you don’t feel it happening. It gets masked as hyper-productivity. Cognitive research suggests that because AI tools make tasks feel easier and enhance visible performance, users are often unable to accurately judge the true status of their own skills. You feel competent, dashboards look green, and then on a Wednesday, a novel incident hits that doesn’t match any pattern the AI has seen, and you realise the muscle has atrophied.

For SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated.

But there’s something even more concerning than deskilling, and researchers have started calling it never-skilling. Deskilling means you once had a capability but have since lost it. Never-skilling means you never developed it in the first place. For junior SREs entering the field today in an environment where AI handles most of the incident response workflow, the opportunities to build foundational intuition and muscle through hands-on practice are vanishing.

The training pipeline itself is broken and not self-healing.

SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult.

We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward.

A few approaches worth considering:

Deliberate inefficiency. Just as the FAA mandates manual flying time even when the autopilot is perfectly capable, SRE teams can designate certain incidents, even the ones the AI could handle, as human-practice opportunities. This can be considered as a long-term investment to keep skills fresh, although it might come at the cost of a super-fast solution

Build for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side. There’s a meaningful difference between a system where a human approves an AI’s recommendation and one where a human actively engages with the problem alongside AI. The former keeps humans in a supervisory role that Bainbridge (the lady who wrote that research paper about 40 years ago) showed leads to vigilance decay, and the latter keeps them cognitively engaged.

Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture.

Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply.

We’re talking about SREs specifically because that’s the world we live in at SigNoz. We build an open-source observability platform, the kind of tool that gives SREs the metrics, traces, and logs they need to understand their systems deeply. For us, this deskilling question is not a rhetorical fad; it directly shapes how we’re building AI into our product.

Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned.

One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would.

And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure.

The future of SRE is human with AI intentionally designed to keep humans sharp, engaged, and ready for the 5% that really counts.

item.title: Florilegium: Procedural Flowers in LaTeX (161 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/kevinraymond/florilegium, See on Hacker News

Origin

The Reddit post asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made, and this project doesn't try to reproduce it. It is one possible way, and the way I did it: hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua, placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look.

What it is

Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden.

Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free.

Two documents share one package, and a third shows what else it does:

florilegium.tex florilegium-grow.tex
composition authored: stems, leaves and flowers placed by hand, every parameter sampled grown: a plant grown to fit the page by a greedy space-filling loop
adapts to nothing (tuned for A4, 68 mm margin) the page layout, and the free space below the text on the last page
preview

Both PDFs are self-describing: the body text is the write-up of how the margin is drawn.

Last page of the grown document: the text ends early, so branches arch into the space below.

300 dpi crop. Mottled washes with white streaks lifted out, lobed leaves with white veins, forget-me-not cymes, a pale ghost flower behind the stems.

Watch it grow

as it grows with the free space it fills

Seed 6, from an empty margin to the finished page. The stems rise first, leaves open as the tips pass their nodes, and each stem ends in a flower. Then the greedy loop takes over: on the right, each dashed circle is the largest free disc it found, just before a branch grows to it. Big holes come first and slowly, small ones last and fast. The butterflies and bees fly in, the bird glides onto its twig, and the snail crawls up its stem until the last frame, which is exactly the page this seed always gives.

The growth is recorded once, while the page is laid out: each stem is also drawn as prefixes of increasing length and each motif at a few smaller scales, replaying the same random draws. A frame then writes the pieces whose time has come, in their original painting order. make grow-6 renders one seed this way (build/grow-6.gif and .mp4, about 45 seconds); add EXPLAIN=1 for the dashed circles.

The margin reads the text

showcase.tex, "A year in the margin": spring on the first page, summer, autumn on the last. Each section describes the feature it shows.

The grown margin can respond to the document around it:

  • Initials. \florilegiuminitial[5]{E} sets the first letter of a paragraph in a tile five lines tall. The outline of the letter is read from an OpenType font (Latin Modern Bold by default) and painted like a petal; a vine passes over and under its strokes in turn, with leaves where they fit and flowers in the gaps, often in the letter's counters. The letter is also typeset invisibly, so the paragraph still copies as "Every".
  • Flowers at the headings. With the option sections, every numbered section and subsection gets a flower in the margin beside its heading, painted in the copper of the accents, the way headings were once picked out in red.
  • A flower where the text asks. \florilegiumbloom puts a flower beside the line it stands in; \florilegiumbloom[lily] asks for any motif of the garden. The marks are found in the page box when the page is shipped out, so this works in one run.
  • Seasons. With the option aging, the garden ages from spring on the first page (mostly in bud, small pale leaves) to autumn on the last (seed heads, falling petals, a few copper leaves). It needs two runs, for the page count; \florilegiumage{0.8} sets an age by hand instead.

One seed in spring, early summer, late summer and autumn. The seasons change what grows, not where.

Visitors

Most pages have visitors: a butterfly or two and bees in the open spaces, a snail crawling up one of the main stems, and on about one page in five a bird perched on a twig of its own. They come from a random stream of their own, so a page without them is exactly the page it would have been; the option novisitors leaves them out.

Any ink

The whole palette comes from one color, ink: Delft blue, sepia, green, crimson, violet, teal. The ramp from the darkest stroke to the palest wash is computed from that hue in OKLCH, so the light end never turns gray.

In PostScript

postscript/florilegium.ps: the grown margin in pure PostScript, one self-contained file. Ghostscript, or a printer, computes every petal while it interprets the page, and the two pages of text explain how.

The drawing core, every primitive and the growth loop are ported from ink.lua, flora.lua and grow.lua, procedure for procedure. It needs no TeX and no other file:

gs -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dSeed=7 -o garden.pdf postscript/florilegium.ps
make postscript             # the same -> build/postscript-7.pdf; SEED=12 for another garden

-dSeed=N picks the garden; without it the clock picks one, so every print is new. -dAge=0 to 1 sets the season, and -dNoVisitors leaves out the butterflies, bees, snail and bird. Two pages take about 2.5 seconds. Much of the Lua maps directly: PostScript's own transformation matrix places each primitive (translate, rotate, scale), paths and Bézier curves are native, and procedures built at run time stand in for Lua's closures (a petal's half-width is a procedure handed to the outline builder). Four things don't map:

  • Layers. The garden grows in one order but is painted back to front, so every fill and stroke is captured with pathforall into a list per layer, and the lists are played back at the end.
  • Transparency. PostScript has none. Ghostscript provides it with -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY. Without that flag, or on a printer, each translucent fill is mixed with the color it is likely to land on and painted opaque. The result is flatter, but it's the same garden.
  • Randomness. The generator is Park-Miller in 32-bit integer arithmetic, and PostScript reals are single precision, so seed 7 here is a different garden from seed 7 in LaTeX.
  • Text. The file typesets its own two pages in Times. It knows where its headings are and where its text ends, so the copper flowers at the headings and the garden under the last line work as they do in LaTeX. It has no initials, animation or authored composition.

The file sent twice to an Epson inkjet with lp postscript/florilegium.ps, with no seed given. The computer's print system runs the program again for each job, so each print takes its seed from the clock and grows a different garden. A printer gets the opaque version, as it has no transparency.

Build

LuaLaTeX, one pass, about a second a page (two passes for showcase.tex, whose seasons need the page count).

make                        # the three PDFs
make seed-7                 # one page from seed 7 -> build/seed-7.pdf
make gallery                # gallery/seeds.png + seeds.gif, inks.png, seasons.png (python3, Pillow, pdftoppm)
make grow-6                 # growth animation of seed 6 -> build/grow-6.gif + .mp4 (ffmpeg)
make grow-6 EXPLAIN=1       # the same with the free discs marked -> build/grow-6-explain.*

No TeX installed? Build the image once and run everything in it:

docker build -t florilegium-tex tools
make RUN=tools/in-docker

Or paste florilegium.sty, the six .lua files and one of the .tex files into an Overleaf project and set the compiler to LuaLaTeX.

Use it in your own document:

\usepackage[grown]{florilegium}      % or plain \usepackage{florilegium} for the authored one
% options for the grown one: sections (flowers at the headings), aging (two runs),
% novisitors (no butterflies, bees, snails or birds)
\definecolor{ink}{HTML}{5B2A1F}      % optional: the hue of the whole palette (this is sepia)
\definecolor{accent}{HTML}{B4662F}   % optional: the copper of the hairlines
...
\florilegiuminitial[4]{T}his paragraph starts with a decorated T.
... a flower in the margin beside this line\florilegiumbloom ...
\florilegiumage{0.8}                 % grown only: autumn from here on
\florilegiumtextend                  % grown only: at the very end of the text

A fixed seed instead of the page number: lualatex "\def\florilegiumseed{7}\input{florilegium-grow.tex}".

Any primitive can be drawn on its own inside a TikZ picture, under the current scope's shift, rotation and scale:

\begin{tikzpicture}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(2,2)},rotate=20]\florilegiumdraw{flower}{1.3}\end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(5,0)}]\florilegiumdraw{leaf}{3.0, {depth=0.6}}\end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(8,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{ghost}{"lily", {s=1.4}}\end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(11,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{butterfly}{1.5}\end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}

How it works

Drawing (ink.lua). All geometry is computed in Lua and written as PDF path operators into one literal node per page; TeX does no arithmetic. Primitives are drawn in a local frame under an affine transform, which is read from TikZ when a primitive is called inside a scope. Colors come from a tone ramp derived from the one document color ink: navy to mist at the hue of ink, interpolated in OKLCH so the light end stays blue instead of turning gray. Tapered strokes are two offset Béziers, not sampled ribbons.

Primitives (flora.lua). Painted in the order a watercolorist would: a flat wash, darker blotches multiplied over it, pigment pooling at the edges, streaks lifted out in white, a few fine veins, and almost no outlines. Broad petals and flowers, star lilies seen at a tilt, blossoms and florets, buds and bellflowers; lobed and entire leaves; forget-me-not cymes that curl like a scorpion's tail, branching sprigs, umbels, tendrils, seed heads; butterflies, bees, snails and a bird; copper sparkles, rosettes and the ivy-leaf fleuron whose stem becomes the head rule. Any of them can be painted as a pale ghost.

Authored composition (authored.lua). A plant grows from a root in the bottom-left corner: three stems through hand-picked control points, a fourth along the bottom of the page as the footer, leaves at chosen fractions of the stems, and every other motif on a branch that leaves its stem tangentially and arrives along the motif's axis — so every flower can be traced back to the root.

Grown composition (grow.lua), in the spirit of Wong, Zongker & Salesin, Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (SIGGRAPH 1998). The stems sway up the column as smooth noise of their height; leaves are hung at their nodes where there is room. Then, repeatedly: take the largest free disc within reach of a stem, choose a motif that fits it, and grow a branch to it from the nearest stem point; the branch becomes a stem in turn. Big holes are taken first, so flowers and lilies land early, sprays and leaves fill the middle, and the loop ends by tucking leaflets, buds and florets onto the stems. The end of the text is measured with \pagetotal in the same pass, so a short last page grows branches into the space below it with one compilation.

Reading the page (florilegium.lua). A heading or \florilegiumbloom leaves an invisible marker node in the text. When the page is shipped out, its box is walked node by node, adding up heights, depths and the glue as it was set, to find each marker's height on the page; the garden then gives those lines their flowers before any leaf is hung. An age reweights the motifs: buds and sprays of buds in spring, seed heads in autumn, when some leaves are painted with a ramp built from the accent instead of the ink.

Initials (initial.lua). The letter's outline comes from luaotfload's OpenType reader as Bézier segments. Flattened into polygons, it gives an even-odd inside test, and a grid of distances to the letter and the frame finds the largest gaps for the flowers. The vine is a Catmull-Rom curve across the tile; where it crosses the letter it goes over and under in turn, and the strands that go over are drawn again, clipped to the letter, with a thin halo of paper.

Procedural ≠ random. The seed is derived from the page number, so page n always gets garden n. Reproducibility is what makes the document stable enough to typeset.

See CLAUDE.md for a handoff-style map of the code, the tunables, and ideas not yet done.

item.title: The federated code forge (178 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://tangled.org/blog/forge/, See on Hacker News

For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation.

But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What has stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however.

Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge.

It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever you choose, you can still talk to everyone else.

Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots, like this one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as mitchellh.com/tack. Go even further and host our ultralight API server and build your own custom forge.

Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the get-go. Tangled is incredibly agent friendly.

The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with it, and to become .

Product updates

A fresh look!

The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look. We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped out Inter for Timeless Sans.

A bobbin near you

Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the appview. The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data and UI rendering using html/template + htmx. It ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden.

This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden, but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer service written in Rust: bobbin. Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring users around the world get the best API and UI performance.

The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services.

The new data model and repo-owned data

First, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now lives under org.tangled.*, replacing the old sh.tangled.* records.

Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in an SSH server in the same binary.

With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are also stored the same way.

In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose.

But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code, so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your project maximum portability.

If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot, the web app also writes an org.tangled.graph.attestation record to your own PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it. Two-way verification!

Self-hosters will have to upgrade their knots to the v1.20.0 by following the upgrade guide.

Organizations

Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They’re passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the New Organization page, and you get <name>.tngl.sh with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories. Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re working on a way to move those over. Read more in the docs.

Stacked PRs for everyone

Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to interdiff between individual changes as well.

Launch weeks ahead

This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your agent.

Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally.

item.title: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance (169 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.npr.org/2026/10/30/g-s1-150902/blockchain-intelligence-firms-link-north-korea-to-6-3b-hack-on-binance, See on Hacker News

FILE - The Binance logo is seen on a smartphone, Feb. 28, 2023, in Marple Township, Pa. Matt Slocum/AP hide caption

Matt Slocum/AP

A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.

The cryptocurrency exchange said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.

The company said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."

TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.

In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.

Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor," its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company's CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on X that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.

Binance said on X it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

item.title: ICE wants its mask back, and hired a company to ask (177 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.flokinet.is/2026/10/29/ice-wants-its-mask-back-and-hired-a-company-to-ask/, See on Hacker News

We receive takedown notices regularly. They come from individuals, lawyers, companies, and governments. This post is part of a series where we document how we handle them, both the routine cases and those that reveal something worth discussing publicly.

This request, to take down icepi.cx (now online again at http://icepicx.is/ ) arrived from a company we have no relationship with, acting for a government agency in a country where we do not operate.

We declined the request.

What happened

The notice describes a doxxing campaign. That is not what the site is.

Doxxing publishes private details about private people so that others can find them at home. Icepick publishes work identities of government employees. Who they work for. What their role is. How they can be reached in that role. The information describes people in the exercise of public authority, not in their private lives. Federal officers carrying out an enforcement programme are not private individuals while they are carrying it out. The public has a legitimate interest in knowing who is doing that work, under whose authority, and in which office. Journalists cannot report on an agency whose personnel are structurally unknowable.

We are not pretending the origin of the data is comfortable. It came from a breach, and nobody in the dataset chose to be in it. The question we had to answer was narrower: does publishing it serve a purpose that a hosting provider should protect? We concluded that it does. The site functions as a reference tool for accountability reporting by journalists and citizens, and that is a use we exist to keep online. This is why we declined the take-down request.

Why this matters

An automated takedown notice does not remove the work of checking whether an accusation is true. It moves that work to the recipient. We made that point about a false accusation from a German police authority, and it holds here with a different agency, a different country, and a different kind of claim.

ZeroFox finds candidate material through AI-driven detection. Whether a given site is accountability journalism or a harassment campaign is exactly the judgment that detection cannot make. Someone has to read the site, look at the dataset, and weigh public interest against personal risk and this morning that someone was us.

This case adds something to that. The party accusing us and the party contacting us are no longer the same. We cannot see who inside ICE decided this site should go, whether anyone did, or what they were shown before deciding. We are being asked to validate a claim whose author we cannot identify.

As a business model, none of this is new. Copyright has worked this way for decades. A private company sells monitoring to rights holders, scrapes for matches, sends demand letters automatically, and takes a share of whatever recipients pay to make the letters stop. Volume is the product. Checking is a cost against it. Plenty has been written about what that does to legitimate speech, and most of it transfers to what arrived in our inbox this morning.

What has changed is the client. In this case its a governmental institution, not a private company. DHS signed a $15 million contract with ZeroFox in July 2026 covering ICE and Homeland Security Investigations, and the company can file on the department’s behalf until 2028. The Intercept reported on a leaked memo describing the programme internally as a “Doxing Mitigation Initiative,” and quoted an ICE official who worried it could be turned on whistleblowers and critics inside the agency rather than on threats from outside it. ZeroFox also has form. In 2015 it classified peaceful Black Lives Matter organisers in Baltimore as “threat actors” warranting continuous monitoring, partly on the strength of their follower counts. The FBI hired the company anyway in 2021.

Validation by the recipient is no longer a side effect of a badly built process. It is part of what the service sells. Finding politically and journalistically relevant information is the product, removing it is the deliverable, and the number of notices filed is the measure of success.

What happened to the site?

By mid-morning, icepi.cx no longer resolved. Its registrar, CentralNic, had placed the domain on serverHold.

Our refusal kept nothing online. The request that decided the outcome to take the site down was not the one sent to us. A registrar reached the opposite conclusion the same morning, published nothing, and a global audience lost access to the site. In the meantime the site is online again under a domain from a different registrar (http://icepicx.is/)

What should be done about this

As we describe in our previous article, legislation like the DSA loads obligations onto hosting providers and asks nothing of the people who file notices.
This case demonstrates what can happen once filing becomes a commercial service available to governmental organisations.

Anyone filing a takedown notice on another party’s behalf should have to state who they act for, under what legal basis, and who is accountable if the claim is wrong. Where a notice was produced by automated detection, that should be declared on its face. A provider cannot weigh a claim properly without knowing whether a human ever looked at it.

Removals at the registry and registrar level need the the same scrutiny.
Enforcement against genuinely harmful content is a legitimate goal, and protecting individuals from harassment is a real one. But a system where an agency can buy removals through a contractor, where the contractor is possibly paid by volume, and where the quickest route runs through infrastructure nobody is watching, like the registrar in this case is not a system for stopping harassment. It is a system for making inconvenient information disappear.
