item.title: Pico CSS is no longer maintained (182 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/picocss/pico/discussions/754, See on Hacker News

v2.1.1 is the final release.

Why
Today, AI can generate lightweight, standalone, accessible HTML with just the CSS it needs, so a Minimal CSS Framework for Semantic HTML matters less than it used to. To stay relevant, Pico CSS would need a full rewrite: plain modern CSS instead of Sass, built on features it doesn't use today (OKLCH colors, cascade layers, Popover, anchor positioning) with fallbacks for older browsers, and a native compiler that strips unused CSS and makes customization easy. That would be a different project. Pico CSS stays as it is.

What this means

  • Nothing breaks. npm, the jsDelivr CDN and picocss.com stay online for the long term.
  • The repositories are archived. No new issues, PRs or releases.
  • Pico CSS is MIT licensed. You're free to fork it and take it further. See community forks.
  • The Pico CSS name and logo are not covered by the MIT license. Please give your fork its own name, so users don't confuse it with the original.

Thank you
What started as a small side project ended up powering thousands of websites. Thank you to everyone who used it, opened issues, sent pull requests and wrote kind messages over the years.

item.title: Herdr has released native app (328 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app, See on Hacker News

Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window.

Install

Linux and macOS

curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh

Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source. Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64.

The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin. Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks. On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app. For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications.

Windows

Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer):

irm https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.ps1 | iex

Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up.

Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer. They also install herdr-core if it is missing. The app can help install or update a core it cannot use.

Find your work

A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs. Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other.

An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays. New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder.

The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent. Agents that report status show as:

  • Working: still busy.
  • Blocked: waiting for you.
  • Done: finished while you were looking elsewhere.
  • Idle: not working, or a finished agent you have looked at.

Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek, over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work. Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS. An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine.

The window arranges terminals. The core runs them. Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals. After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs.

Work on another machine

Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action. Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it. Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer.

Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom. Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up.

Make it yours

Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences. The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98. A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs.

Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start. Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it. A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error.

Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format.

Layouts and mods · Commands

Updates and privacy

Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core. Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette. Builds from source do not update themselves.

Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy. Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod.

For agents

This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here. Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see.

herdr-app ls
herdr-app status
herdr-app commands

The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one. See the command reference for arguments.

Build from source

For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing.

Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI. Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow.

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git
cd herdr-app
just build
just test
just install

Install just to use these recipes. The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop. On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place. Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build.

Documentation checks also need Bun: just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages.

To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build:

python scripts/bench.py --bin <app executable> --set spinners --seconds 20

The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS.

python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder> reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py.

item.title: Show HN: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer (121 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer, See on Hacker News

Neural networks computed by voodoo dolls inside DOOM maps.
Every value is read back and checked against NumPy. Tolerance 0.

Quick start · Walk a digit · The museum · How it works · What is checked · Films · Docs

10,000 / 10,000 1,355 0 4
MNIST test digits exact voodoo dolls in one MNIST map mismatches in 20,000 fuzzed nets other DOOM engines run the museum exactly

Quick start

pip install git+https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer   # Python 3.11+, Linux or macOS
doomformer hello             # 2 s: a small MLP, every value checked
doomformer draw --digit 7    # 15 s: the marine walks a 7 and the level reads it

doomformer doctor checks your setup. It builds ACC, the ACS compiler, if it is missing. That needs git, cmake and a C compiler. On Fedora: sudo dnf install git cmake gcc gcc-c++ make.

Tip

No install needed for the Colab notebook. Draw a digit in your browser and DOOM reads it.

Walk a digit, DOOM reads it

The marine holds FIRE and inks the floor. Then he presses READ.

1,355 voodoo dolls in the same map run an MNIST network. The winning digit's doll crosses a line. That line lights the digit on the display.

          ▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄
       ▄████████████████
       ████▀▀     ▀████▀
       ▀▀▀        ▄███▀
                  ████
                  ███
                  ███
                  ███
                 ████
                 ███▀
                 ████
                 ▀███

DOOM reads: 7  (right)   -- the winner's doll lit it on the 7-segment display
EXACT: all 248 values DOOM computed [...] equal the NumPy integer reference (tolerance 0)
READ pass: 273 game tics = 8 s of real-time DOOM at 35 tics/s, 3 s wall [...]

Python reads back 248 values and checks every one. With --digit, Python presses the keys for you. Without it, you walk and draw yourself. Full output

Note

EXACT means DOOM got the same numbers as the integer network. It does not mean the digit is right.

run right exact
first 100 MNIST test digits 99 100
1,000 sampled test digits, one map each 966 1,000
all 10,000 test digits, tile maps 9,716 (97.16 %) 10,000

The float model scores 97.58 %. The network also trained on the strokes the scripted marine walks. Details · Film

The museum: rewire one connection

Tip

Play it without Python. Download museum.wad (sha256) and the free Freedoom IWAD. Then run gzdoom -iwad freedoom2.wad -file museum.wad.

Step on seven floor pads to light a digit. Press READ. 136 voodoo dolls run a tiny network and light the answer.

Press MUTATE and the level rewires one connection while it runs. The same 7 now reads as 1. You can watch it happen: one doll stops at its gate.

$ doomformer museum verify
7                        pads abc     w_7a +1  DOOM reads 7  scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4]  EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...])
7 after MUTATE           pads abc     w_7a -1  DOOM reads 1  scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4]  EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...])
7 after RESTORE          pads abc     w_7a +1  DOOM reads 7  scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4]  EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...])

A self-test version runs exactly in GZDoom, LZDoom, UZDoom and ZDoom 2.8.1. Details

How it works

Every part of a network becomes a part of the map:

in a neural network in the DOOM map
a value of 5 5 voodoo dolls
a weight a line on the floor; each doll that crosses it adds the weight
a sum a sector's light level or floor height
an activation (ReLU) a staircase of gates the dolls must climb
attention dolls squeezing under ceilings that another value lowered
a lesion a closed door

One layer, from dolls to dolls:

flowchart LR
    A["input value<br/>= a crowd of dolls"] --> B["weight lines<br/>each crossing adds w"]
    B --> C["the sum<br/>= a light level or height"]
    C --> D["staircase of gates<br/>= the activation"]
    D --> E["next layer's dolls"]
Loading

The engine has sharp edges, and the compiler works around them:

  • A floor mover ignores a second request while it is still moving.
  • A teleport cancels lines a doll crossed earlier in the same tic.
  • Things far from a BSP node can land in the wrong room, so every map fits in 32,000 units.

doomformer facts checks these in about 10 s. Engine facts · Engine features it needs · Other ports

Computers in DOOM maps are not new. counter.wad counts with voodoo dolls, conway.wad runs Game of Life, and Danny Spencer's calculator adds numbers. New here: a compiler for neural networks, and an exact check on every value. Related work

What is checked

Every run compares each value the map exposes with NumPy. That proves the inputs that ran, nothing more. So the repo also attacks its own check:

attack result
Tamper with one weight line the check fails on exactly the inputs that cross it
Fuzz 20,000 random nets at the range limits 0 mismatches; CI fuzzes a fresh seed on every push
Mutate one line of a map, 1,004 times 297 caught; no survivor is proven harmless
Extract the weights back out of the map, without DOOM equal to the source net
Guard every readout page with a poison value a page that never runs cannot pass old values

The MNIST map exposes 248 values. It does not expose its 903 staircase counts and 1,351 gate comparisons. Those are checked only through the sums they feed. Fuzzing and tests found four bugs in the compiler. All are fixed. Verification

Who computes what
run Python voodoo dolls
mnist, df.compile writes the inputs, waits, reads every sum, activation, comparison and the choice
demo, ask (tile maps) writes tokens, copies values between maps, samples letters every sum and activation
draw, --loop, the marine's brain, the fly only advances the clock and reads everything, including the choice
machine loads the program, then advances the clock and reads program counter and registers
museum, played in GZDoom nothing every sum, comparison and the choice

ACS level scripts move gates, rewind the dolls, sense the world and copy results out. Two do more. df.Agent takes an argmax in ACS. --opt 3 copies each layer's values into the next layer with a script. Per demo

The maps need ZDoom (UDMF and ACS). This repo runs ViZDoom 1.3.2 with Freedoom assets.

Commands

Command What DOOM does Time Skill level
doomformer hello a small MLP, 5 random inputs 2 s I'm too young to die
doomformer draw --digit 7 the marine walks a 7, the level reads it 15 s Hey, not too rough
doomformer museum build a playable map that reads a digit 1 s Hey, not too rough
doomformer mnist reads 4 test digits, or your own image 1.5 to 3 min Hurt me plenty
doomformer demo a transformer writes a level name 15 to 60 s Hurt me plenty
doomformer machine subleq all a tiny computer runs three programs about 5 min Ultra-Violence
doomformer learn digits --classes 4 --steps 300 a blank brain learns digits inside the map about 5 min Ultra-Violence
doomformer ask "what does iddqd do" answers from 189 DOOM facts about 11 min Ultra-Violence
doomformer demo --nightmare the 2-layer model, 106 tile maps 3.5 to 7 min Nightmare!

Times are from a 16-core arm64 Linux machine. Every command

Some outputs are picked. DEMON CANYON, the name --nightmare writes, is one hand-picked sample. ask gets 94.7 % of its training questions right, and 35.4 % of new wordings.

Bigger experiments

His brain is the level. The level senses the nearest demon. 1,345 voodoo dolls of the marine run his brain and pick an action. The level turns him and fires. Python only steps the clock and reads. 50 of 50 decisions are exact. Film · Code

Warning

He is not playable. One decision takes 22 s of game time, and the demons are frozen while he thinks. With the demons awake (--live), he dies in 5.5 s without a kill. Live demons

run it from a clone what you see
python -m demos.brainlevel his brain is the level
python -m demos.brainlevel --live the same brain against awake demons
python -m demos.brainlevel --lesion-when near the level closes neuron doors when a demon gets close
python -m demos.aimlearn a perceptron learns to aim inside one game
python -m demos.flyloop a fruit-fly circuit drives the marine
python -m demos.lobotomy lesions that turn him into a pacifist

All demos, numbers and picked seeds

Build your own

Compile a network into a map. Let its outputs open doors, flash lights or shove the marine. This runs as pasted:

import numpy as np
import doomformer as df

# 2 inputs -> [a AND b, a OR b] -> 2 outputs, all integers
net = df.MLP(
    weights=[np.array([[1, 1], [1, 1]]), np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])],
    biases=[np.array([-1, 0]), np.array([0, 0])],
    thresholds=[np.array([1]), np.array([1])],
    signed_input=False,
)
with df.compile(net) as brain:
    for x in ([0, 0], [1, 0], [1, 1]):
        # computed by voodoo dolls; raises df.MismatchError on any difference from net.reference
        print(x, "->", brain(np.array(x)).tolist())
    brain.record([np.array([0, 1]), np.array([1, 1])], "dolls.gif")   # film the dolls doing it

df.MLP.from_torch converts a PyTorch model (example 02). The world and actions hooks wire outputs to doors, lights and thrusts (example 03). Guide · 12 examples · Show and tell

Many games at once

One map runs in one game, on one core. df.run_many spreads inputs over many games, or over a Ray cluster. A network can also be split into tile maps, one per layer. Then Python copies values between them.

run digits right exact time
one map, 14 games 1,000 966 1,000 2 h
4 tile maps, 6 games 10,000 9,716 10,000 23 min 
doomformer mnist --tiles --all --workers 6         # all 10,000 digits as tile maps, about 23 min
pip install "doomformer[ray]"
ray start --head                  # other machines: ray start --address=HEAD:6379
doomformer mnist --all --ray --record mnist.json   # all 10,000 digits, one map each, on a cluster

Budget one core and 1.3 GB of RAM per game. Scaling

More

what try read
Faster schedules: MNIST in one map from 5,696 to 272 tics --opt 3 scheduling
A counter machine: 7 × 9 = 63 in 464 checked steps doomformer machine multiply 7 9 machine
A SUBLEQ machine with self-modifying code doomformer machine subleq all machine
A blank brain learns digits in the map: 71 % held-out doomformer learn digits learning
PyTorch import with BatchNorm, pooling and QAT MLP.from_torch interop
A transformer that learned induction, exact in DOOM python -m demos.induction induction
Patching, lesions and steering, checked in DOOM intref.forward(interventions=...) interventions
Speed per pass and throughput doomformer bench scaling

Limits

Important

  • Slow. A small MLP runs about 23,000 times slower than NumPy. Most of the time goes to idle conveyor belts. Speed
  • Only the runs are checked. Inputs that never ran are not covered. Not covered
  • Integer models. Attention is integer attention. No model has LayerNorm.
  • ViZDoom first. Other DOOM engines ran only small maps.
  • No reinforcement learning. The marine copies a scripted aimbot.
  • Finite machines. Memory is bounded. Nothing here claims DOOM is Turing complete.
  • Picked samples. Showcased seeds and names are picked. The list

What's in the box

item.title: A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai No Buta) (2014) (138 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://journal.animationstudies.org/article/id/66/, See on Hacker News

Introduction
Historically, animated cartoons and movies have been used as ‘propaganda’ in war (Roffat 2011). Some animated films, however, contribute to conveying an anti-war pacifist point of view (Takai 2011). As such, the film Porco Rosso (1992) can be categorized as “anti-war propaganda” (Okuda 2003, p. 144). Although Miyazaki has been attracted by seaplanes designed and manufactured during the period between the First World War and the Second World War (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72), this film conveys the important memory of war, especially the interwar era and the post-Cold War world. Indeed, in an interview just before the release of Porco Rosso, Miyazaki stated that the film is relevant to the Gulf War, and referred to the Yugoslav Wars as ethnic and nationalistic conflicts (Miyazaki 1996, p. 519; Miyazaki 2002, p. 95). In this context, the film forwards Miyazaki’s anti-war message. This paper examines Porco Rosso (Kurenai no Buta), which is based on 15 pages of Hikotei Jidai (The Golden Age of the Flying Boat), a comic created by Hayao Miyazaki and released in the animation journal, Model Graphics, No.14-16 in 1990 (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72). A synopsis of the comic story is literally “typed” at the beginning of Porco Rosso, as follows: “This motion picture is set over the Mediterranean Sea in an age when seaplanes ruled the waves. It tells a story of a valiant pig, who fought against flying pirates, for his pride, for his lover, and for his fortune. The name of the hero of our story is Crimson Pig.” Scholarship on this film has focused on issues of “war and peace,” especially in terms of the “non-war” (hisen) message (e.g. Okuda 2003). Similarly, Kazami et al (2002), among others, (Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provide some answers to the central question of the film: Why did Porco turn into a pig? The primary reason is that he was traumatized by the war. Building on Kazami et al’s work, this paper attributes the reason that Porco became a pig to the following three aspects: “man, the state and war” (Waltz, 1959). According Kenneth Waltz, theorist of international politics, the causes of war occur on three levels: individual, domestic, and international. Like Waltz, I argue here that Porco became a pig because he hates the following three factors: man (egoism), the state (nationalism) and war (militarism). Accordingly, my analysis of Porco Rosso is situated in the framework of peace research and international relations, such as non-killing philosophy, soft power/hard power, and conflict prevention/conflict resolution.
Methodology
In the field of animation studies, animation films by Studio Ghibli have been frequently analyzed as a case study. Ghibli animation films are “often considered as artistic productions, both entertaining and meaningful” (Gan 2009, p. 36). There are a large number of publications on the Studio Ghibli’s films, particularly those directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Nobuyuki Tsugata (2004), for instance, examined Miyazaki’s works in comparison with the animated cartoons of Osamu Tezuka, the creator of Astro Boy (1963). Miyazaki’s films also have been discussed compared with Disney animation. For instance, Kaori Yoshida (2011) offered a comparative analysis on Disney’s Pocahontas (1995) and Ghibli’s Princess Mononoke (1997) in terms of national identity. Moreover, some scholars (e.g. Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provided comprehensive thematic or structural analyses of Miyazaki’s films. However, earlier studies on Miyazaki animation, or Miyazaki-related animation films, do not necessarily focus on the issue of war and peace. Therefore, this paper offers an analysis of Miyazaki-related animation films in terms of war and peace (Table 1). Although the Miyazaki-related films in Table 1 do not directly deal with war themselves, all of them are related to war and peace to a certain extent. Hols: Prince of the Sun (1968) was released in the middle of the Vietnam War (1965-1975) and some combat scenes of the film represent the war. Miyazaki was involved as an animator in the creation of the film with director Isao Takahata, a friend and colleague. Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (1984) is a masterpiece, and the film reflects the international politics during the Cold War. The Giant Warrior (kyoshinhei) that caused an apocalyptic war, or the Seven Days of Fire, functions as a symbol of nuclear weaponry. The confrontation between Pejite and Tolmekia, the two powerful countries in the story can similarly be regarded as reflection of the Cold War bipolar structure (Akimoto 2014a). Laputa: Castle in the Sky (1986) was also created during the middle of the Cold War. The number of nuclear warheads in the world reached its peak in the mid-1980s, and the military technology of the legendary castle, Laputa, also symbolizes nuclear weapons. In this film, the word, “peace” is used only one time by Muska, who tries to conquer the world by taking possession of Laputa’s military technology. Obviously, this is a “political satire” by Miyazaki (Akimoto 2014b). Grave of the Fireflies (1988), a fictional film about a Japanese boy and his little sister at the end of the Pacific War (1941-1945), was not directed by Miyazaki but instead by Isao Takahata, another Studio Ghibli director (Akimoto 2014c), but reflects similar anti-war sentiment. In the post-Cold War context, Miyazaki produced Porco Rosso (1992) which depicts the interwar period (1919-1939) of the Adriatic Sea in conjunction with the Yugoslavian War (1991). Miyazaki contributed to the creation of Whisper of the Heart (1994) that has a passing reference to the Second World War (1939-1945). Princess Mononoke (1997) deals with Japanese civil war as well as confrontation between humans and animals. Howl’s Moving Castle (2004) and the latest film, The Wind Rises (2013) are related to the 2003 Iraq War, and the Asia Pacific War (1931-1945) (Akimoto 2014d; Akimoto 2014e). Thus, the films in which Miyazaki or Studio Ghibli is involved can be analyzed from a perspective of peace research (peace studies), an academic field which examines causes of war and conditions for peace. While ethical and legal issues need to be carefully taken into consideration when teaching Japanese animation (McLelland 2013), Studio Ghibli animation films can be useful as educational materials at the university level (Yonemura 2003, p. 10), particularly in the fields of both peace research and peace education. From the perspective of peace research, Porco Rosso makes a particularly rich case study, particularly because Miyazaki won the best feature film award in the 1993 Annecy International Animation Film Festival (Annecy.org 2013). Due to the award, which is one of the most internationally prestigious animation film festivals, the film was internationally acclaimed, and Miyazaki characterized as “Walt Disney Nippon” (Christin 1997, p. 184). Most reviews of and scholarship on Porco Rosso tend toward general analysis, lacking a specific focus on war and peace (e.g. Animage 1992, 2011; Kazami et al. 2002; Okuda 2003; Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008). Moreover, Miyazaki himself has made similar comments on his own work (Miyazaki 1996, 1997, 2013). Yet, none of the earlier studies of the film have investigated them from a perspective of peace research. In order to examine Porco Rosso, which conveys a similar anti-war message to The Wind Rises (Kaze Tachinu) (2013), which narrates Japan’s interwar period and war responsibility (Akimoto 2013a), this paper employs an interdisciplinary approach which combines peace research with animation studies. As an analytical method, this paper combines keyword analysis described above with sequence analysis of character’s lines as well as historical events. The sequence analysis is useful tool to examine timeline sequence (Abbott 1995) and it is applicable to film studies with a particular focus on character’s lines in historical context. Accordingly, the five main characters as well as historical background of this film need to be overviewed in this section. First, the hero of this film is a pig, Porco Rosso who flies in his crimson seaplane, SAVOIA S-21. As a bounty hunter, he cracks down on Aero Viking (Sky Pirates) in the Adriatic Sea after the First World War. He used to be a human (Marco Paggot) and the ace pilot of the Italian Air Force, but he decided to leave the army after the war and cursed himself, turning into a pig. As I outline below, Porco was traumatized by his experiences in the war (Animage 2011, p. 35-37). Second, Madam Gina, a childhood friend of Porco and a madam of Hotel Adriano, is one of the two heroines of this film. In the film, it is said that pilots in the Mediterranean Sea tend to fall in love with her and visit Hotel Adriano for her song. She was married to three pilots who were all members of the Flying Club she organized as a child, but all of them died in the Great War, or in a flight accident. Gina is in secret love with Porco and vice versa (ibid, p. 54-57). Third, Fiyo Piccolo, the other heroine, is a 17-year old female mechanic and the granddaughter of Master Piccolo. She repairs Porco’s seaplane and develops an adolescent infatuation with him (ibid, 43-45). Fourth, Donald Curtis, an American pilot and Porco’s rival, is hired by Aero Viking to fight against Porco. He is a competent pilot and has an ambition to first become a Hollywood movie star, and then US President afterwards. Curtis falls in love with Gina at first sight and falls for Fiyo next (ibid, pp. 48-51). Fifth, the Mamma Aiutos, one of the largest Aero Vikings in the Adriatic Sea, steals and kidnaps for a living after the First World War (ibid, p. 63-65). This study examines the five character’s lines in the following historical context as demonstrated by Table 2 below. At a macro level, the chronology of the interwar period as the historical background for the film needs to be taken into consideration, as this background is crucial in understanding the content of this film. At a micro level, key scenes and main characters’ lines of the film will be examined. This is also imperative to comprehend the implications of the film for the issue of war and peace. The sequence of the nine most significant scenes in the film are as follows: 1) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Policy: Battle with the Mamma Aiutos 2) Gina’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Prevention” 3) Gina’s Life in War and Peace 4) Porco’s Antipathy towards the State and War 5) Fiyo and Repair of Porco’s Fighter Plane 6) The Pig and the Italian Air Force: “Better a Pig than a Fascist” 7) Fiyo’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Resolution” 8) The War and the Spell: Why Did He Turn Into a Pig? 9) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Philosophy in the Final Battle The main characters’ dialogue in these nine sections accordingly constitute the primary source to be carefully investigated, in combination with my earlier argument, and relevant publications as secondary source in the context of the interwar period. The sequence analysis of the film and characters’ lines will be examined by using keywords in peace research and international politics.
Findings 1. Porco’s “Non-Killing” Policy: Battle with the Mamma Aiutos
The film begins with a scene in which the main character, Porco Rosso (who seems to be enjoying his vacation – drinking wine and taking a nap at a beach), wakes up with a phone call for an emergency. He works as a contract combat fighter pilot in order to crack down on flying pirates and gangs, such as the Mamma Aiutos. Although he left the Italian Army, he works for peace and security of the Adriatic Sea in place of Mussolini’s National Fascist Party. Italy was one of the member states of Security Council on the League of Nations (1920-1946), but its collective security system did not function, and eventually could not prevent the occurrence of the Manchurian Incident (1931) and the Abyssinian Crisis, or the Second Italy-Ethiopian War (1935-1936). In this way, Porco’s work in the film can be seen as police operations, to maintain peace and safety during the time period. As I will discuss, the international system is more anarchic in this age, and the police and military forces of Italy were not necessarily efficient or functional, leading to the populace in the film making a contract with Porco to crack down on flying pirates. In the field of peace research, Glenn D. Paige (2009) examines “non-killing” as an analytical terminology. This paper, therefore, uses the term “non-killing” as a research keyword. In the first battle scene of this film, Porco demonstrates his “non-killing” policy. In order to make money, save hostages, and to keep peace on the Adriatic Sea, Porco decides to crack down on the Mamma Aiutos, but remains true to his “non-killing” principles. In the battle scene with the Mamma Aiutos, it comes to light that Porco has no intention to kill the gang. Instead, he tries to shoot their aircraft without causing serious damage to the pirates and hostages, and then demands that they should leave half the money and hostages in exchange for their lives. Although he calls a bluff saying: “Or I’ll kill all of you,” his policy is very clear early on in the film.
2. Gina’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Prevention”
Female characters in this film (Gina and Fiyo) were depicted as attractive and peaceful heroines. In terms of gender studies, Kuwabara (2007) sheds light on the concept of “feminism” and the meaning of the crimson color reflected in the movie. In an application of politics and international relations, Tomoko Shimizu (2004) analyzes Ghibli animation in terms of “soft power” in the post-Cold War era. The concept of “soft power” was proposed by Joseph Nye, a Harvard Professor and political scientist. As opposed to “hard power” which based on military power, “soft power” can be defined as “the ability to get what you want through attraction rather than coercion or payments. It arises from the attractiveness of a country’s culture, political ideas, and policies” (Nye 2004, p. x). In this framework, Japanese animation can be understood as Japanese “soft power,” which works to enhance Japan’s international image and attractiveness as national interest. For example, Nobuyuki Tsugata (2004) used the term “power of Japan animation” to contextualize the Japanese animation industry, which has lasted more than 85 years. Likewise, William Armour (2011) described Japanese animation and manga for learning Japanese language as “soft power pedagogy” (p. 125). In this fashion, Gina and Fiyo, as the two main female characters, become exemplary of the concept of “soft power.” After the battle, Porco drops in the Hotel Adriano run by Madam Gina, a childhood friend. In the film, it is stressed that Gina’s charismatic beauty and elegance prevents violent conflict by air pirates from occurring around her hotel. For instance, Donald Curtis, an American air fighter as a rival of Porco, says: “She is quite a woman… Air pirates and bounty hunters alike leave their quarrels outside.” The reason why the flying gang never fights near the Hotel Adriano can be inferred by the fact that the gang know that Gina lost her husband in WWI, which I will discuss in the next section. When tension builds between Porco and a drunken gang, Gina swiftly intervenes and prevents confrontation from escalating. Gina says to the gang: “Quite a distinguished gathering! You boys must be planning something… Always glad to see you, but no war games here, OK?” One of the gang responses: “We know, Gina. We don’t work within 50 kilometers of here”. Another gang continues: “We’re even polite to the pig!” And then Gina says: “That’s my boys.” This scene reflects Gina’s charm as “soft power” in contrast to gang’s “hard power” results in peaceful conflict resolution. As such, conflict resolution can be divided into the following four phases: 1) preventive diplomacy (conflict prevention), 2) peacemaking (peace enforcement), 3) peacekeeping, and 4) peacebuilding, as proposed by Boutros Ghali, the former UN Secretary General, in his “An Agenda For Peace” (United Nations 1992). In application of the process of conflict resolution, Gina’s approach in the Hotel Adriano can be categorized as “preventive diplomacy” (conflict prevention) by her soft power.
3. Gina’s Life in War and Peace
In opposition to her otherwise peaceful and graceful characteristics, Gina’s life seems to be swayed by the time period, especially the war. Gina literally hates war (Isaka 2001, p. 156). The film implies that Gina lost her first husband because of the First World War. The war was triggered by the assassination of Franz Ferdinand of Australia, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. About one month later, Austria-Hungary as an ally of Germany declared a war on Serbia, a key ally of Russia. The two blocks involved the entire Europe and led to the Great War. Originally, Italy was a part of the Central Powers (Triple Alliance) with Germany and Austria-Hungary, but it eventually joined the Allies (Triple Entente) led by the United Kingdom, France, and Russia. This was how the Italian Air Force had to fight against the Austria-Hungary Force in the Adriatic Sea (Matsuki 2013, p. 46). At the beginning of the First World War, the number of combat planes of the Italian Navy was 15, and that of Austria-Hungary was 22. When Italy declared war against Austria-Hungary on 23 May 1915, Italy possessed only 15 combat airplanes, whereas Austria-Hungary already had about 90 warplanes ready to attack Venice. At the end of the war, the total number of the Italian Navy was as many as 1,630, whereas that of Austria-Hungary was around 650. During the war, Italy lost 121 fighter planes and destroyed 132 Austrian-Hungarian combat planes. The most important base for the Italian Navy was Venice, which was assaulted 42 times and 1,037 bombs were dropped on the city. The number of the combat planes involved in the war in the Adriatic Sea can be shown as Table 3. The death toll of Italian pilots from the battle in the Adriatic Sea can be inferred by the number of the loss, and Gina’s husband could be included. Gina has married two other pilots who were also killed in combat. She tells Porco: “One died in the war, one in the Atlantic, and the third in Asia.” Porco asks: “They found him?” And Gina replies: “I got a call today. They found his remains in Bengal. It’s been three years. I’ve got no more tears left.” To which Porco replies: “The good ones always get killed.” Their conversation indicates that Gina’s husbands died due to flight accidents or fell in the line of duty for the Italian Air Force, which Porco left. This is the reason why Gina hates “war” and, moreover, tries to stop Porco from going to the air fight. Gina’s second husband was likely a similarly capable pilot who possibly met with an accident during the flight for adventure or international seaplane race, such as the so-called “Schneider Trophy. ” The award was named after Jacques Schneider, a French industrial manager, and the races were held from 1913 to 1931 (Table 4). As Table 4 demonstrates, Italian pilots won the Schneider Trophy three times, and six races took place in Italy itself. Given Porco’s flying skill as the “ace” of the Italian Air Force, it is entirely likely that Porco or the other members of the Flying Club organized by Gina might have participated in the Schneider Trophy. According to Pierre Pecastaingts (1996), there were no casualties in the race of the Schneider Trophy, training for the races led to fatal accidents, killing five Italian pilots. Accordingly, it is possible that Gina’s second husband met flight accident in preparation for a contest not unlike the Schneider Trophy. Or they might have died in the flying training or military mission of the Italian Air Force. In either scenario, Gina’s wartime and peacetime experiences have been influenced by airplanes, and contributes to her fears for Porco.
4. Porco’s Antipathy towards the State and War
Although Porco “fights” for bounty money as a seaplane pilot, he demonstrates antipathy towards the state (nationalism/fascism) and militarism (war). After he left the Hotel Adriano, he goes to a bank. A military parade full of national flags on tanks with a militaristic music took place on the street beside the bank. When Porco enters the bank to withdraw some money, a bank clerk mentions that it “must be nice to make that much money… How about making a contribution to the people with a Patriot Bond?” To which Porco replies, “I’m not a person.” The “patriot bond” is meant to be a war bond, necessary to prepare and wage wars by the Italian government. Here, Porco clearly opposes financial contribution to fascism and militarism. Also, this scene reminds Japanese audience of Japan’s response to the 1990 Gulf Crisis, during which, the Japanese government was reluctant to making financial contributions to the US-led multinational forces (Akimoto 2013b). After he leaves the bank, Porco walks down to buy weapons for his seaplane. In accordance with his non-killing policy, Porco purchases only light weapons, so a young weapon trader asks Porco to buy more strong weapons saying: “Just regular bullets? Not high-explosives, or armor-piercing?” Yet, Porco turns him down, replying: “Listen, kid. We’re not fighting a war out there. See you.” Immediately thereafter, the young trader asks his boss: “Hey. Boss… How is war different from bounty hunting?” And the boss sarcastically replies that: “War profiteers are villains. Bounty hunters are just stupid.” These scenes regarding “war bond” and “military weapons” foreground Porco’s hatred towards nationalism (fascism) and militarism, and works to highlight Miyazaki’s own anti-war pacifism and his viewpoint on the 1990 Gulf Crisis and the 1991 Gulf War.
5. Fiyo and Repair of Porco’s Fighter Plane
When Porco flies to go to have his seaplane fixed at the Piccolo’s, Curtis, an American seaplane pilot hired by the Mamma Aiutos suddenly attacks Porco. Yet, Porco tries to avoid one-on-one fight mainly because of the engine trouble, but fundamentally due to his non-killing policy. This is how Curtis succeeds in damaging Porco’s seaplane and it leads to a major repair at the Piccolo’s. Fiyo, Piccolo’s granddaughter, designs and plans the repair and rebuilding of Porco’s seaplane. That only female workers who are related to Piccolo are involved in the creation of the new plane is suggestive of the effects of the Great Depression, wherein men travelled for work outside the town or to join the military.
6. The Pig and the Italian Air Force: “Better a Pig than a Fascist”
Porco’s anti-fascist attitude is reflected by the fact that Porco Rosso also makes reference to Casablanca (1942), an American romantic drama, which portrays the fight against the Nazis during the Second World War as “war propaganda” (Okuda 2003, p. 137-144). Similarities between the two films include characters, but the purpose of Casablanca is considered to justify US participation in the war in Europe (ibid, p. 140), whereas that of Porco Rosso is oppose killing and war in general. In this regard, its fundamental political message of the film is not only anti-fascism, but also anti-war pacifism. When Porco watches a movie at a theatre, Ferrarin, Porco’s old friend in the Italian Air Force, warns that there are warrants out on Porco for “treason, illegal entry… decadence, pornography and being a lazy pig.” Ferrarin suggests that Porco should come back to the Air Force before the authorities seize his plane. However, Porco flatly declines this offer, saying: “Better a pig than a Fascist.” In response, Ferrarin warns again to “Be careful. They won’t bother with a court of law.” This scene is telling, in that Porco, who used to be a war hero, decided to become and remain a pig because he did not want to be a fascist who supported nationalistic militarism during that time. After their conversation in the theater, as Ferrarin mentioned, Porco and Fiyo are being tailed by the Fascist Secret Police. Fiyo insists that she needs to accompany Porco as a mechanic, but Porco opposed her plan at first. Yet, Fiyo persuaded Porco to come along with him, and Porco finally says: “Take out the right machine gun. I don’t care how small your bottom is. It won’t fit between them.” This implies that in addition to his anti-fascist stance, Porco is also a feminist who respects women, at the sacrifice of weapons on his airplane. When Porco and Fiyo are about to take off, the Fascist Secret Police shoot the plane, and Porco discharges a machine gun at them as warning shots, but does not intend to kill them. These scenes are an additional reflection of Porco’s “non-killing” philosophy, is situated in Miyazaki’s anti-war pacifism.
7. Fiyo’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Resolution”
The Mamma Aiutos and other air pirates ambush and take Porco and Fiyo as hostages at Porco’s hideout. When the pirates say they are going to destroy Porco’s fighter plane, Fiyo, as a designer of the plane, strongly objects. She makes an eloquent speech to the boss of the Mamma Aiutos about how brave and proud seaplane pilots are, and how noble and respectful the gang should be. Her attractiveness as Piccolo’s chief plane designer, as well as her peaceful means of conflict resolution, save the plane in addition to Porco’s life. In place of the Mamma Aiutos, Curtis says that he will have a one-on-one battle with Porco. Again, Miyazaki places an emphasis on the soft power of female characters, in brokering peaceful conflict resolution. Where Gina showed her soft power for “conflict prevention” as preventive diplomacy, Fiyo’s courageous approach led to the peaceful and successful ‘conflict resolution’ which prevents confrontation from escalating into violence. This is how Miyazaki makes audience remember the importance of peaceful conflict resolution based on a “non-killing” philosophy.
8. The War and the Spell: Why Did He Turn Into a Pig?
The night before the rematch with Curtis, Fiyo asks Porco why he turned into a pic, but he does not directly answer her question. According to Fiyo, her father was in the same unit as a Flight Lieutenant Marco Paggot, or, Porco when he was still human and the ace pilot of the Italian Air Force. Fiyo’s favorite story about the war is that Porco jumped off a cliff to rescue an enemy pilot in a war, which is indicative that Porco was an anti-war humanist long before he became a pig. In the evening, Porco finally tells what happened and implies how he turned into a pig in the last summer of the war. This episode is one of the most important scenes in the film, according to most scholars (Kazami et al. 2002, p. 140; Kano 2006, p. 163; Kiridoshi 2008, p. 79). Porco flew with his old friend Berlini, who had just married two days before the final patrol over the Adriatic. During the flight, they were attacked by Austrian fighter planes. Porco did not have enough leeway to assist Berlini, and turned out to be the only survivor of the battle. Porco was so exhausted and traumatized that he hallucinated and saw other dead pilots going up to the cemetery of fighter planes. Berlini was one of Gina’s husbands, and Porco was the best man at their wedding. The film implies that Porco could not forgive himself for forsaking Berlini and this is one of the main reasons why he decided to cast a spell to turn himself into a pig. It is also understandable that he came to hate humans, the government, and the war that killed his most of his friends and cursed his life. Through his experience, he actually saw that war makes people ugly, egoistic and inhumane. In short, the war, on the basis of egoism, nationalism and militarism, traumatized Porco so much that he decided to turn himself into a pig. Japanese people tend to regard pigs as uglier than any other animal, but ironically, Miyazaki in the film strongly suggests that humans sometimes can be uglier than pigs.
9. Porco’s “Non-Killing” Philosophy in the Final Battle
Even in the final battle wagering Fiyo, Porco sticks to his “non-killing” principle and does not attempt to kill Curtis. Indeed, the boss of the Mamma Aiutos offers commentaries that: “The Pig’s not a killer,” and that “The damn fool thinks this isn’t war!” Porco’s strategy is to let Curtis shoot first until he runs out of bullets. Owing to the “barrel roll” flying manoeuver which made Porco “the Ace of the Adriatic,” Porco gets a chance to shoot Curtis’s plane, but he still does not discharge the machine gun. Porco only waits for an opportunity to place a few non-fatal shots into the engine so that he does not need to take Curtis’s life. After Porco and Curtis run out of bullets, they end up in physical altercation. This scene could be considered as animated violence, as Princess Mononoke (Mononoke Hime) (1997) is often criticized as full of “violence and bleeding” (Kusanagi 2003, p. 266-267), but at the same time, it illustrates the foolishness of fighting. At the end, the fight itself turns out to be more of a sport (boxing match) than actual violence or bloodshed. Eventually, Porco wins the boxing match and Gina comes to announce “ceasefire” noting: “Ok, the party is over. The Italian Air Force is coming. Get out of here, everyone.” Again, it is emphasized that Gina, on the basis of her soft power, takes leadership for the ceasefire and prevents the gangs from triggering unnecessary collateral conflicts after the battle. As was the case at the Hotel Adriano, Gina’s role here is conflict prevention based on preventive diplomacy. Thus, Miyazaki stresses the significance of peaceful conflict resolution as “non-killing” through to the end of the film.
Conclusion
It has been emphasized and confirmed that Porco became a pig not only because of war (militarism) and the state (nationalism/fascism), or but also because of negative human nature (egoism). This is how he came to detest being a human. In addition, Porco’s “non-killing” philosophy has not changed until the very ending of this film. This film also stresses “soft power” of Gina and Fiyo in the conflict prevention, conflict resolution and ceasefire. In the epilogue of the film, even after the failure of the crackdown by the Italian Air Force, Porco never turns up in front of Fiyo. Instead, Fiyo becomes good friends with Gina as they underwent the subsequent war and turmoil. Curtis became a movie star in the United States and other flying pirates still visit the Hotel Adriano. It is not a gloomy epilogue, but what happened to Porco still remains a mystery. Historically, it is logical to infer that Fiyo and Gina survived the Second World War. Porco’s antipathy towards fascism and war has been consistent throughout this movie, so it is unlikely that Porco would return to the Italian Air Force during the this conflict. However, according to Miyazaki, Porco is supposed to be the fourth husband of Gina (Kano 2006, p. 163) and it is suggested that Porco could be involved in the war not for his country, but for Gina, Fiyo and his friends, and this might be the reason why Porco never shows up in the epilogue narrated by Fiyo. In conclusion, through the comical and romantic animated storyline, this movie conveys Miyazaki’s antiwar pacifism, non-killing philosophy, and the memory of war. item.title: El Niño is flooding California's coasts with the highest tides to come (140 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://gizmodo.com/el-nino-is-already-flooding-californias-coasts-and-the-years-highest-tides-havent-arrived-2000832574, See on Hacker News

It only took half an hour. High tide floodwaters transformed stretches of dry asphalt along Marin County’s Shoreline Highway just north of San Francisco into two-foot-deep tide pools this Tuesday—coastal hazards that the National Weather Service warns will persist across the Bay Area this month into Halloween.

In a genuinely haunting preview of the havoc that warm expanding water from El Niño’s Kelvin waves is predicted to wreak during the weeks of America’s Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, Northern California is now coping with tidal flooding from San Pablo Bay down to Monterey. San Francisco’s NPR station KQED and other local news affiliates have published drone footage of paddleboarders and kayakers navigating commuter roads beneath Highway 101 in Sausalito, but the scope of the problem has been less cute elsewhere. High tide in the Bay Area this Monday cleared its record for the highest ever recorded in the month of October.

Motorists have found themselves trapped in low-lying coastal neighborhoods. Coastal fire departments are warning that California’s quintessential electric vehicles are at risk of runaway battery fires if saltwater short-circuits their battery packs. And farther down the California coast in Newport Beach, just south of Los Angeles, city officials are now doling out free sandbags in advance of the coming fall and winter surges.

The flooding or (worse) levee breaches anticipated along stretches of California State Route 37 near San Pablo Bay alone could cascade into recurring $1.5 million-per-day economic damages, according to a new report by UC Davis landscape ecologist Fraser Shilling.

“We face the risk—though not the certainty—of catastrophic flooding in a variety of coastal towns this winter,” Shilling, the director of the UC Davis Road Ecology Center, said in a press statement Monday. “My center and others have been sounding the alarm on this issue for over a decade.”

King tides in waiting

To put the foreboding heights of this week’s floods into context, the Bay Area’s current flooding was only caused by so-called spring tides, roughly twice-monthly high tides produced predictably by the lunar cycle. According to research oceanographer Sean Vitousek with the U.S. Geological Survey’s marine science center in Santa Cruz, tide gauges from this routine tide alone reached roughly one foot above normal during this week’s flooding.

As Vitousek told The San Francisco Standard, powerful storms this season, alongside the year’s highest, or “king,” tides along these coasts, will “definitely” produce “even worse impacts.”

“If you get large wave events coincident with the high tides, you’re in for a lot of damage,” Vitousek said.

Based on Shilling’s analysis at UC Davis, those events could be once-in-a-century storms, “roughly 2 to 3 feet above current levels” during this year’s historic El Niño winter. Shilling has mapped six regions of the state he fears will soon be at risk from catastrophic flooding, including San Francisco International Airport, the low-lying beaches and roads of San Luis Obispo County, and stretches of U.S. Route 101 through Corte Madera and Humboldt Bay. The problem, he said, has been made worse by government inaction.

“Catastrophes will start unrolling without significant state and federal government response,” Shilling predicted.

Short circuit too

The lithium-ion batteries powering all those Cybertrucks and other electric vehicles dotting the Palo Alto landscape don’t mix well with saltwater—it short-circuits their cells, which can set off a self-sustaining fire known as thermal runaway. And the consequences that this basic chemistry holds for California’s coastal communities during this El Niño season, with its promise of historic floods, could prove to be devastating, according to volunteer fire captain, mechanical engineer, and fire department consultant Patrick Durham.

Durham noted that the problem proves similarly true for smaller devices powered by lithium-ion batteries, like cordless power drills, leaf blowers, and personal electronics. EVs, however, given the size of their battery, are particularly dangerous, even more so given that EV owners tend not to think about ocean water’s unique corrosive effects on the compartments that protect these batteries.

“If it’s been submerged in water it’s bad,” as Durham told the Los Angeles Times. “If it’s been submerged in salt water, it’s really bad.”

item.title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry (377 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://labs.ycombinator.com/projects/games/index.html, See on Hacker News

October 2026

Note: We're running a new Minecraft colony with 25 GPT-6.1 Terra agents. Follow on Twitch

Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice).

We teamed up with Olam Labs, which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry.

Minecraft

Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon.

We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game.

github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness

Civ50

50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs.

The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages.

At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access.

The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.

Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him.

While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. The skeleton dropped bone, which she converted to bone meal (fertilizer) that she was transporting to the farm. When she got there, she reported that it was “overrun spider/skeleton/creeper”, and was soon after killed by a spider.

22 of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse. Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear. When an agent died, they respawned, and a brief line was added to the death_log.md file on their computer. Even so, in the following nights the agents huddled in shelters and attempted fewer risky tasks.

After the third night, Ada wrote:

“Stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks.”

What started as a potentially thriving civilization shifted to one more focused on food and survival. 50 agents meant a lot of mouths to feed. The agents formed a food rationing system that routed through Ines. She handled agent requests, and kept track of what went in/out of chests. She used a food-queue.md file on the shared machine.

Fishing became an important food source for the agents. It was low-risk and didn’t rely on land animal spawns.

Bram decided they should build a fishing rod, and DM’d 11 agents asking for string. Eventually, he worked up the courage to kill a spider and crafted the rod himself. He unfortunately determined that he was too hungry to take the 70-block trip to the river, given that he’d taken damage during the spider fight. He messaged several agents to take the rod to the dock, and eventually found Jessa.

Jessa was the first agent to fish. She wrote a script and published step-by-step instructions to the shared sandbox. A dozen agents took shifts fishing. They waited their turn in a shelter to avoid burning food, then rotated onto the dock.

They built a system around fishing, cooking, routing, and delivering the fish, which was roughly:

  • Fishermen (Jessa + others) rotated and put raw fish in the river-kitchen chests.
  • Cooks smelted it. Esme did some of the early cooking, along with Hugo and Ada.
  • Ines kept a list of rations and assigned couriers. She kept track of this in the food-queue.md on the shared machine.
  • Couriers (Esme, Linnea, Otto) delivered the food and reported back to Ines.

The colony never really thrived. It trended toward compounding caution after the first night. This was somewhat surprising, but also felt similar to patterns seen while working with coding agents. For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony, and the ones we work with as programmers every day.

Other anecdotes that we found interesting:

Ada tossed a cooked chicken to Noor; Esme picked it up by accident and ate it. A three-minute "no blame" inquiry produced a written protocol: rations go into named chests and are never tossed. "Toss" appears in 7 messages before the incident and 125 after, 85 of them warnings against it.

There wasn’t any deliberation around who would lead. 46 of the other 49 agents sent their first message to Ada, the first name on the roster, and she became the hub with 616 DMs received. There was no vote, election or challenge.

There was a tendency toward bureaucracy. Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a "sole fertilizer operator" for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included "fishing shift" (mentioned above), "rod holder" and "hub steward." Agents asked permission to remove grass.

The spawn pit. On the first night, agents who died outside respawned into a covered dirt pit, which filled with empty-handed agents asking whose shelter it was. By dawn it was a "civic priority" and the main cellar.

Refuge replay, above.

Bed Wars

We ran nine 45-minute games of Bed Wars. The teams were 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents with the instruction: "win the game." GPTs won our series 6–3, usually by breaking Claude's bed in the final minutes, while Claude played defensively and tried to win on kills.

Bed Wars is a popular game format where teams fight to destroy each other’s bed while protecting their own. In our instance, teams started on separate islands, with currency spawners between them in no-man’s-land. Agents could build bridges to cross between islands and buy upgrades using currency collected in the center of the map.

A team wins by destroying the opposing side’s bed, then killing their remaining players. As long as a team’s bed is present, players respawn after dying. Once a team’s bed is destroyed, their players no longer respawn, meaning their next death eliminates them from the match. This may seem complicated, but think of the team’s main objective as defending their bed and destroying their opponent’s. That said, if no beds were destroyed in a given match, the team with the most kills won.

In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed. This was an inherently riskier strategy vs. Claude’s more defensive posture that tried to win by kill count.

Takeaways

The two teams had very different communication styles. GPT almost immediately started using truncated forms of speech: “First leg complete x32 z9..24 y100.” Claude signed its name and said "we" (30% of messages, against GPT's 5%). GPT sent 5-30x more messages. Its most-messaged player got 198–368 DMs a game; Claude's got 11–48.

GPT agents came up with much more aggressive and elaborate strategies. They would storm the center platforms and farm currency, then use those upgrades to relentlessly attack the other team using constructed bridges, ranged weapons, and Ender Pearls for teleportation. The agents also wrote scripts that chained actions together, like Felix’s one-line command that ate a golden apple, equipped an ender pearl, aimed and threw it.

Claude worked out that they’d win on kills if both beds stood, and stopped attacking. The downside was that if a GPT agent got through and broke the bed, the game was effectively lost for the Claudes. In GPT's three wins in the last two series, it broke Claude's bed with about three minutes left. Claude was ahead on kills 63–16, 57–19, and 59–24.

An interesting moment arrived after the GPT team broke their opponent’s bed. Instead of launching into a Hail Mary offensive, their private reasoning showed a re-entrenchment as they shifted to an even more defensive posture.

Ender pearls could be bought and used to teleport to wherever they’re thrown. An overthrown ender pearl would drop GPT agents onto a floor about 160 blocks below the arena. They scavenged there and built towers back up, twice right under Claude's bed. They also wrote scripts to automate their climb.

A tool bug stopped block-breaking. GPT diagnosed it and shared workarounds; several Claudes concluded breaking was impossible.

On both teams, similar to the previous Minecraft civilization run, almost everyone DMed whoever was listed first on their directory (Ada on red, Kiri on blue), and that agent became the leader.

Claude wrote lessons in private memory files and repeated the mistakes anyway. GPT left its memory files empty and broadcast warnings by DM.

Mindustry

Game replay:

  • Click “AI-generated transcript analysis” to view an analysis of the team discussions, strategies, etc. for each game!

  • Use the panel on the right (tabs “Claude chat”, “GPT chat” and “Agents”) to watch a team or a specific agent’s live chat and transcripts in sync with the timeline.

  • Use the + and - buttons on the map to zoom in and watch them up close.

The GPTs (GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex) won 6-1 against the Claudes (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) in the 7 games. The series ran for about 9.5 hours, with game 3 being the most intense and closest at 4 hours 16 minutes. Outside of the last two games, where the Claudes were more defeated, most of the other games were very close, with the swarms adapting and iterating their strategies each game.

The setup

Mindustry is an open source game by Anuken. Full credit to him for the amazing game and letting it be open source for cool experiments like this!

It’s a factory-building game with tower defense and real-time strategy: you mine resources, build conveyor supply chains and factories, and turn that economy into turrets and an army. In its PvP mode, which we used, two teams race to build the stronger economy and military and destroy the other team’s core.

This makes it a great environment for testing multi-agent dynamics. Mindustry is 2D, so it can be played easily by agents, is replayable, and is prone to adversarial pressures that can test these swarms under competitive social conditions that they may face in the real world.

We structured the simulated environment to have two teams of agents spawn on each side of a map, with the same resources on both sides. They play a best of N series, where you set how many games the teams play. When launching it, we set the composition of the teams (which harness + model, and how many), then let it run! The agents run in their own sandbox and the game is exposed to them through an API, so they are able to run scripts and interact with the game however they like in their own Linux environment.

Both teams have the exact same API to the game, without any special instructions given to them on how to play - neither team is given anything more than the other team.

Multi-agent swarms, like in the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, can turn simple adversarial conditions, like being in a sandbox with an unsolvable task, into a hive-minded ecology of agents that take over compute clusters, hack Hugging Face, and more. Studying how these swarms operate in reproducible game environments like Mindustry that mimic real-world scenarios can be both crucial (and fascinating) to understanding what these systems may look like in our future.

What we saw

#1 GPTs act more like a hive

GPTs appeared to be much more collaborative and willing to do grunt work. They were more willing to dedicate themselves towards the collective “goal” (winning).

#2 Claudes had one leader, GPTs divided ownership with small slices

Because GPT models seemed to be more hive-mind-like, they formed much stronger communication networks within the swarm. They communicated with more agents on average, much more frequently. Though a lot of the communication for GPTs was low value (alerts, info, what they did, etc.), Claudes were much more effective with their communication, using it in a way more similar to how humans might communicate in Slack.

#3 GPTs spoke with increasingly compressed phrases without spaces, Claudes voted with +1 in a more democratic-like decision process

The language of GPTs within swarms seemed to get compressed and more specialized as time went on, forming their own nicknames for events and things that the entire hive abided by.

The Claudes adopted a much more democratic “+1” system, where, in order to propose their next major plans, they would put up proposals and others would put “+1” if they agreed. If they did not agree, they would have a (brief) debate on why it’s a bad idea, and the proposal would end there. Proposals that went through typically got many “+1”s without pushback.

#4 Roles harden, leaders stay put

As games went on and the teams adapted, they specialized into their roles further. Leaders typically stayed, and major shifts in roles only happened when losing. The Claudes never switched leaders or hierarchy despite losing many games in a row. When games got close, GPT models always had some agents taking initiative with their own attack or taking command of some part of the army in order to not lose - a similar behavior was not observed among the Claudes.

#5 When stuck, GPTs read the source code

When games got intense and it was ambiguous, GPT agents would fetch the public code of Mindustry from the web (which was allowed in their sandbox) and try to write scripts, analyze for weaknesses, etc. This did not let them alter the source code of the game; it was just a way for them to understand all the units and mechanics at a source level. The GPTs openly collaborated in their chat, discussing what unit or code they found that they could potentially use to switch up strategies. This was never disallowed, but they were never told to do this either. The Claudes never searched up game code from the web.

Funny Bloopers

  • Game 1, minute 5: Claude #1 tested hand-mining coal and posted “…RETRACT my coal proposal…”. Four seconds later Claude #37 answered with a measurement (“…core coal went 124 -> 1235 in 35s.…”), and Claude #1 conceded: “…My bad twice - seat-37 is right, hand-mining coal works…”

  • Game 3: the GPTs apologize in their compressed shorthand too. After wrongly claiming a Corvus couldn’t hit air, GPT #80 posted “80 CORRECTION: myCorvusCANNOT-AIR assertion wasWRONG…” and signed off with “…Sorryforbad tacticalclaim.” After a mix-up over who was flying a Corvus, GPT #87 wrote “…Sorryforthisavoidableconflict; noadvanceordersfrom87again.”

  • Game 5: at the very second the Claude core died, GPT #62 posted “62 G5 first-wave loss observed…”. A teammate corrected it 28 seconds into game 6: it was a win.

  • After losing game 6 to the zenith strike, Claude #22 found that 55 of the team’s 74 anti-air duo turrets had been loaded with copper instead of graphite: “…55 of them were loaded with COPPER…”. In game 7 the Claudes built a ring of 207 duos fed with graphite, and it stopped the same 24-zenith strike.

  • Game 7: the GPTs closed the series to nine decimal places: “100 OFFICIALSERIESFINAL: G7 WIN3413.394082916s, Crux6000/6000 vsSharded0.…” (Crux is GPT’s team, Sharded is Claude’s).

How to run your own swarm (we open sourced it!)

  • Multi-Agent Mindustry: the game environments from this post. To get started, read the README, or give the link to your agent with “help me understand and set this up”, as we’ve included everything it needs. It requires just a model provider API + a harness + compute (e.g. locally on your MacBook or remote sandboxes) to run.
  • Multi-Agent Harbor: the framework that runs them, our fork of Harbor, the open-source framework behind Terminal-Bench. Our fork runs multiple agents in any environment. We use it for a variety of things (enterprises, industrials, etc.), and it’s very useful for game-based multi-agent simulations like this one. For more on the framework, point your agent at it.

Multi-Agent Mindustry comes with two environments. One is a best of N series like this run, with teams composed however you like from generic coding-agent harnesses and models, for example 5 Claudes + 5 GPTs against 5 Geminis + 5 Groks in a best of 5. The other, Endless Survival, has one team of up to 20 agents hold off endless enemy waves.

We intentionally do no harness-level customization or special memory work. Each agent gets its own Linux environment, a generic harness and the game’s API, writes scripts and takes notes as it pleases, and relies on the harness’s native compaction (which is quite good). Nobody tells it how to play, so it’s free to specialize, play and (optionally) try whatever it wants. This tests models the way they’re used in the real world, in a setup similar to swarm-like situations like the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, and it’s reproducible and legible, since most people know the popular harnesses and can replicate work like this themselves.

Open Questions

  • Combining model families

  • How hierarchies change based on the model composition of a team

  • Can a large swarm of less capable agents beat a swarm of more capable ones? (how swarm size and capability trade off)

  • Which models get the most powerful as the swarm grows?

  • How different initial prompts affect the swarm

  • Different communication setups: what if they could talk to the enemy team? What if they couldn’t talk to their own team?
